title: Bullying, Harassment & Sexual Harassment Policy
summary: What bullying, harassment and sexual harassment are, Opal Therapy's positive duty to prevent them, how to report, and what happens next — including harassment by participants and their families, not only by colleagues.
body:
BULLYING, HARASSMENT & SEXUAL HARASSMENT POLICY

1. OPAL'S POSITION AND ITS DUTY

Nobody at Opal has to tolerate being bullied, harassed or sexually harassed at work — by a colleague, a manager, a participant, a family member, a support worker or anyone else encountered in the course of the work.

The law now requires more of an employer than a complaints box. Under the positive duty in the Sex Discrimination Act, Opal must take reasonable and proportionate measures to eliminate sex discrimination, sexual harassment and hostile workplace environments, so far as possible. Under the Work Health and Safety Act 2020 (WA), bullying and harassment are psychosocial hazards Opal must control like any other risk. Both duties run continuously, and neither waits for a complaint.

2. DEFINITIONS

2.1 Bullying is repeated unreasonable behaviour directed at a worker that creates a risk to health and safety. Examples: persistent belittling or criticism, spreading rumours, exclusion, setting impossible deadlines, withholding information needed to do the job, unjustified threats about job security, and aggressive or intimidating conduct.

2.2 Harassment is unwelcome conduct related to a protected attribute — sex, race, disability, age, sexual orientation, gender identity, religion, pregnancy, family responsibilities and others — that a reasonable person would anticipate could offend, humiliate or intimidate.

2.3 Sexual harassment is any unwelcome conduct of a sexual nature in the same circumstances. It includes sexual comments and jokes, staring or leering, unnecessary physical contact, sexually explicit messages or images, repeated invitations after a refusal, intrusive questions about someone's private life, and sexual assault, which is also a crime.
It does not have to be repeated, it does not have to be directed at a particular person, and it does not depend on the intention of the person doing it.

2.4 Sex-based harassment is demeaning conduct of a seriously offensive nature directed at a person because of their sex, even where nothing sexual is involved.

2.5 Victimisation is subjecting someone to detriment because they made, supported or might make a complaint. It is treated as seriously as the original conduct.

2.6 What this is not. Reasonable management action carried out in a reasonable way is not bullying — allocating work, setting performance expectations, giving fair feedback, managing underperformance, or investigating a complaint. Being managed is uncomfortable sometimes; that alone does not make it bullying.

3. HARASSMENT BY PARTICIPANTS AND FAMILIES

This does happen in home-based clinical work, and it is not part of the job. Sexualised comments, propositions, exposure, unwanted touching, persistent personal questions, racist or homophobic remarks, or intimidation by a family member are all reportable, whatever the person's disability or circumstances.

If it happens: end the session if you can do so safely, leave, and report it the same day. You will be believed and supported. Opal will consider whether the service continues, whether it continues with a different arrangement, and what conditions apply. Nobody is required to keep attending an environment where they are being harassed, and no participant's needs outweigh a worker's safety.

4. WHAT TO DO

4.1 If you feel safe to, and only if you want to, you can tell the person the behaviour is unwelcome and ask them to stop. You are never obliged to do this first.

4.2 Report it to your supervisor, or to [TO CONFIRM: the named contact for bullying and harassment complaints and their details]. If your concern is about that person, report to [TO CONFIRM: the alternative contact].

4.3 Write down what happened while it is fresh: dates, times, what was said or done, who else was present.

4.4 You can report on behalf of someone else, or report something you witnessed. Bystanders who say something are part of how this is prevented.

4.5 You can also go outside Opal at any time: the Fair Work Commission for a stop-bullying or stop-sexual-harassment order, the Australian Human Rights Commission, the WA Equal Opportunity Commission, WorkSafe WA, or the police where a criminal offence may have occurred.

5. HOW OPAL RESPONDS

• We take every report seriously and treat it confidentially, sharing only with those who need to know.
• You will be told what will happen, and asked what outcome you are seeking. Where the conduct is serious, we may need to act even if you would prefer we did not, and we will tell you if that is the case and why.
• Informal resolution is available where it is appropriate and both people want it. It is never used for sexual harassment or for serious allegations.
• A formal investigation is fair to everyone: the person complained about is told what is alleged and given a real opportunity to respond, and findings are made on the evidence.
• Interim measures — changing reporting lines, adjusting a roster, reallocating a participant — are protective, not punitive, and are not a finding against anyone.
• Outcomes range from an apology and training through to dismissal, and to a report to police or a regulator.

6. NO VICTIMISATION

Any detriment toward a person who reports, supports a report or participates in an investigation is itself a serious disciplinary matter, separate from whatever the original complaint was about.

7. PREVENTION

Training at induction and refreshed at [TO CONFIRM: refresher frequency]. Bullying and harassment risk is assessed as a psychosocial hazard under the Work Health and Safety Policy. Reports and near misses are reviewed for patterns by [TO CONFIRM: role responsible].

title: Gifts and Benefits Policy
summary: When you may accept a gift from a participant or a supplier, when you must decline, what has to be declared, and how to refuse graciously without hurting someone who is genuinely grateful.
body:
GIFTS AND BENEFITS POLICY

1. WHY THIS IS NOT TRIVIAL

Two very different things get called a gift. A participant handing you a jar of homemade jam at the end of a long piece of work is one. A supplier funding your conference attendance while you are writing equipment recommendations is the other. The first is a relationship to be handled with care; the second is a conflict of interest wearing a friendly face.

2. THE TEST

Before accepting anything, ask:
• Could this reasonably look like it might influence my professional judgement?
• Would I be comfortable if the participant's family, my colleagues, the NDIS Commission or a journalist knew about it?
• Is this person in a position where they may feel they have to give me something?
• Is this a pattern, or a one-off?

If you hesitate on any of them, decline or declare.

3. GIFTS FROM PARTICIPANTS AND FAMILIES

3.1 May be accepted without declaration: a token of low value, given as thanks, at the natural end of a piece of work — chocolates, flowers, a card, baked goods, something handmade. Share it with the team where you can; that is usually the spirit it was given in.

3.2 Must be declined: money in any form, gift cards and vouchers, alcohol above token value, jewellery, electronics, anything of significant value, anything given repeatedly, and anything given before or during a decision that affects the participant — a report, an equipment recommendation, a funding submission.

3.3 Never, under any circumstances: a loan in either direction, a bequest or inheritance, property, being named in a will, or any involvement in a participant's financial affairs. See the Professional Boundaries Policy.

3.4 Declaration threshold: anything valued above [TO CONFIRM: the declaration threshold, commonly $50] must be declared in writing to your supervisor and recorded in [TO CONFIRM: the gifts and benefits register and who maintains it], whether you accepted it or declined it. Recording a decline is as useful as recording an acceptance.

4. HOW TO DECLINE WITHOUT CAUSING HURT

Someone who has saved up to buy you something is not trying to compromise you, and being refused can feel like rejection. Say something true and warm: that you are not allowed to accept it, that the rule exists to keep things fair for everyone, and that what would mean the most is feedback about the service — or a note we can share with the team.

If declining would cause real distress to a person for whom giving is culturally significant, accept it, declare it, and discuss it with your supervisor. Cultural context is a legitimate consideration and it is a reason to consult, not a loophole.

5. SUPPLIERS, VENDORS AND OTHER PROVIDERS

Held to a stricter standard, because the risk is direct.

5.1 Acceptable: product information, genuine clinical education, a working lunch at a training session, product samples for clinical evaluation that are logged.

5.2 Not acceptable: commissions, referral fees, kickbacks, or any payment linked to recommending a product; travel, accommodation or conference attendance funded by a supplier without written pre-approval; entertainment, event tickets and hospitality beyond a modest working meal; personal discounts on products you recommend professionally; and gifts to your household.

5.3 Every offer from a supplier is declared, accepted or not, under the Conflict of Interest Policy.

5.4 Where an equipment recommendation is involved, the comparison of options goes in the participant's file — what was considered, what was recommended, and why. That record is the answer to any later question about influence.

6. GIFTS FROM OPAL TO OTHERS

Do not give a gift, discount or benefit to a participant, a family member or a referrer that could look like an inducement. Opal does not pay for referrals. Small acknowledgements to another organisation — a thank you, flowers after a bereavement — are approved by [TO CONFIRM: who approves gifts given on Opal's behalf].

7. IF YOU GET IT WRONG

If you accepted something you should not have, say so. It is usually fixable — return it, donate it, or declare it late. An unreported gift discovered later looks like concealment, however innocent it was.

title: Professional Boundaries Policy
summary: Where the line sits between a therapeutic relationship and a personal one, why the responsibility for holding it is always the clinician's, and what to do when a boundary has already been crossed.
body:
PROFESSIONAL BOUNDARIES POLICY

1. WHY THIS POLICY EXISTS

Occupational therapy is delivered in kitchens, bathrooms and bedrooms, often over months, often to people who are isolated. Warmth is part of the work and rapport is a clinical tool. That is precisely why the boundary needs to be explicit: the conditions that make this work effective are the same conditions in which boundaries erode without anyone deciding to cross one.

2. THE PRINCIPLE

The relationship exists for the participant's therapeutic benefit and for nothing else. There is a power imbalance in it — over access to supports, over what gets written in a report, over a funding recommendation — and it does not disappear because the relationship feels equal or friendly.

Holding the boundary is always the clinician's responsibility. It is never the participant's, and it is not shared with them. A participant may initiate anything at all; the professional obligation to decline is unaffected.

3. WHAT IS NOT PERMITTED

3.1 Sexual or romantic involvement with a current participant. No exceptions, no consent defence, and no "it was outside work hours". This includes flirtation, sexualised comments, and sexual or intimate touching that is not clinically necessary and explained.

3.2 A relationship with a former participant, or with a family member or carer of a current participant, where the therapeutic relationship or the participant's vulnerability is a factor. Discuss any such situation with your supervisor before it develops, not after.

3.3 Financial entanglement. Lending or borrowing money, selling anything to a participant, accepting a loan, involvement in their financial affairs, acting as their power of attorney, being a beneficiary or witness to their will, or accepting any inheritance or bequest.

3.4 Providing services to your own family members or close friends, or treating your own relative as a participant, except where it is discussed and documented in advance with your supervisor as the only reasonable option.

3.5 Using information from the therapeutic relationship for any purpose outside it.

4. WHAT NEEDS JUDGEMENT AND SUPERVISION

Some things are not prohibited but need to be thought about, and the test is always: does this serve the participant's therapy, or does it serve me?

• Self-disclosure. A short, purposeful disclosure can build rapport. Detailed disclosure about your own life, problems or health shifts the participant into supporting you.
• Physical contact. Clinically necessary contact is explained and consented to before it happens. A hug initiated by a participant is not an emergency, but repeated physical affection is a pattern to raise in supervision.
• Contact outside sessions. Personal phone number, personal email, messaging apps, out-of-hours contact. Use Opal channels. If a participant contacts you personally, redirect them and record it.
• Social media. Do not connect with participants or their families on personal accounts. See the Social Media Policy.
• Gifts. See the Gifts and Benefits Policy. Small tokens of thanks may be accepted in some circumstances; money, valuable items and anything given repeatedly may not.
• Extra help. Giving a lift, running an errand, doing a small job around the house. Well-intentioned and frequently the beginning of an unsustainable pattern. If a participant needs it, it belongs in their plan, not in your goodwill.
• Small communities. In rural and regional practice you will meet participants at the shops, the school and the football. Acknowledge them, follow their lead about being recognised, and do not discuss anything clinical.

5. THE WARNING SIGNS

You are being asked to notice these in yourself. In order of seriousness, roughly:
• Thinking about a particular participant outside work more than others.
• Looking forward to one participant's sessions differently, or dreading a different one.
• Sessions consistently running long with one person.
• Keeping something about the relationship out of your notes or out of supervision.
• Telling yourself this participant is a special case.
• Doing things for one participant you would not do for another, or that you would not want a colleague to see.
• Feeling that you are the only one who understands them.

None of these makes you a bad clinician. Not mentioning them does.

6. WHAT TO DO

6.1 Raise it in supervision, early. This is what supervision is for, and raising it is the expected professional behaviour rather than a confession.

6.2 If a boundary has already been crossed, tell your supervisor immediately, and stop. Reporting it yourself is treated very differently from it being discovered.

6.3 If a participant behaves toward you in a way that crosses a boundary — sexualised comments, persistent personal contact, romantic overtures — you do not have to manage it alone. Report it. Your safety and comfort matter, and the participant may need support with the underlying issue.

6.4 If you have a concern about a colleague's boundaries, raise it. Under the NDIS Code of Conduct that is not optional, and under the National Law a notification to AHPRA may be required.

7. CONSEQUENCES

A sexual boundary violation is grounds for immediate dismissal, mandatory notification to AHPRA, notification to the NDIS Commission where applicable, and referral to police where a criminal offence may have occurred. Other boundary breaches are handled proportionately, and self-reported ones are handled as supervision and learning wherever they safely can be.

title: Information Security & Acceptable Use Policy
summary: How to use Opal Therapy's systems, devices and accounts safely — passwords and multi-factor authentication, email, mobile devices, remote work, AI tools, what is monitored, and what to do the moment something goes wrong.
body:
INFORMATION SECURITY & ACCEPTABLE USE POLICY

1. PURPOSE

Opal holds health information about people with disability. It is among the most sensitive categories of personal information there is, and the practical consequences of losing control of it fall on people who are already vulnerable. This policy is the set of habits that keeps that from happening.

2. WHO AND WHAT THIS COVERS

Everyone who uses an Opal account, device or system, including contractors and students. It covers Opal-owned equipment, personal devices used for work, and any account created for Opal purposes.

3. ACCOUNTS AND ACCESS

3.1 Your account is yours alone. Never share a password, never let someone work under your login, and never log in on someone else's behalf. Every action is attributed to the account that performed it, and that attribution is the audit trail.

3.2 Passwords. Long and unique for every service. A passphrase of several unrelated words beats a short complex string. Never reuse a password you use elsewhere, and never write one down where it can be found. Use the password manager if one is provided: [TO CONFIRM: approved password manager, or note that none is provided].

3.3 Multi-factor authentication is required wherever it is available, and is not to be disabled. If MFA is asking you to approve something you did not initiate, deny it and report it immediately — that is an attacker with your password.

3.4 Access is granted on least privilege. Ask if you need access you do not have. Do not use access you do have for a purpose outside your role, and do not look up records out of curiosity: every access is logged.

3.5 Tell us promptly when someone leaves or changes role so their access can be changed the same day.

4. DEVICES

4.1 Lock your screen every time you walk away. Set an automatic lock of no more than [TO CONFIRM: screen lock timeout].

4.2 Encryption and passcode on every device that touches Opal information, including a personal phone with Opal email on it.

4.3 Keep operating systems and applications up to date. Install updates when prompted rather than deferring them indefinitely.

4.4 Never leave a device visible in a vehicle. Take it with you or lock it out of sight before you arrive, not at the destination.

4.5 Personal devices. Where you use one for work, you accept that Opal information on it must be protected to this standard, that Opal may require it to be removed when you leave, and that a lost device must be reported. Do not store participant files locally on a personal device.

4.6 Public Wi-Fi is not to be used for participant information without [TO CONFIRM: whether a VPN is provided and required]. Tethering to your own phone is safer than a cafe network.

5. EMAIL AND MESSAGING

5.1 Use your Opal account for all work communication. Do not forward Opal mail to a personal account.

5.2 Check the recipient before you send. Misaddressed email is the single most common privacy breach in health services, and autocomplete is how it happens. Slow down on anything containing participant information.

5.3 Send the minimum. Use initials or a participant ID rather than a full name and address where the recipient will still understand.

5.4 Phishing. Be suspicious of urgency, of a request to change bank details, of an unexpected attachment, and of a login page reached through a link. Verify by phoning a number you already have, never a number in the message. Report anything suspicious to [TO CONFIRM: who to report a suspected phishing email to] and do not delete it until told to.

5.5 Do not use personal messaging apps for participant information.

6. AI TOOLS

Opal's portal includes AI-assisted features that operate under governance controls: logged, subject to a kill switch, and bounded to Opal's own systems. Use those.

Do not paste participant information, employee information or Opal's confidential material into any external AI service — a general chatbot, a transcription site, a document summariser, a translation website. Text entered into a consumer AI service leaves Opal's control, and treating it as a disclosure is the correct assumption.

Anything an AI feature produces is a draft you are responsible for checking. See the Clinical Documentation Policy.

7. WORKING REMOTELY AND IN THE COMMUNITY

Position your screen so it cannot be read over your shoulder, in a cafe, a waiting room or a participant's living room. Use headphones for calls and do not take a clinical call where you can be overheard, including at home if others are present. Do not print at home unless there is a secure way to destroy it.

8. PAPER AND PHYSICAL SECURITY

Minimise it. Do not leave documents in a vehicle overnight. Return them the same day. Secure destruction only — a household bin is not disposal. Keep the office locked and do not prop external doors.

9. ACCEPTABLE USE

Reasonable personal use of Opal systems is fine — a personal email at lunch, a bit of browsing. Not acceptable: anything illegal; pornographic, violent or discriminatory material; running a private business; installing unapproved software; circumventing a security control; or using Opal's systems to harass anyone.

10. MONITORING

Opal may monitor and log use of its systems, including access to participant records, email metadata, and security events. This is done for security, safety and compliance, not for general surveillance of staff, and access to logs is restricted. You should not expect privacy in what you do on Opal's systems.

11. WHEN SOMETHING GOES WRONG

Report immediately — a lost or stolen device, a misdirected email, a suspected phishing click, a password you think has been compromised, a record accessed by the wrong person, a ransomware message.

Report it to [TO CONFIRM: the person to notify of a security incident, and an after-hours number]. Report a suspicion, not a conclusion; the assessment clock under the Notifiable Data Breaches scheme starts when someone becomes aware something might have happened.

Do not attempt to fix it quietly, do not delete evidence, and do not pay anything to anyone.

Reporting a mistake you made will not, on its own, lead to disciplinary action. Concealing one will.

12. WHEN YOU LEAVE

Return every device, key and card. Opal information is removed from personal devices. Your accounts are disabled on your last day, and your confidentiality obligation continues indefinitely.

title: Work Health and Safety Policy
summary: Opal Therapy's duties and yours under the Work Health and Safety Act 2020 (WA) — the hazards that actually arise in mobile community occupational therapy, how we control them, and how to raise a safety concern.
body:
WORK HEALTH AND SAFETY POLICY

1. PURPOSE AND COMMITMENT

Opal Therapy is a person conducting a business or undertaking under the Work Health and Safety Act 2020 (WA), and owes a primary duty of care to ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, the health and safety of workers and of anyone else affected by our work.

Most of our work happens in other people's homes, in cars, in schools and in community settings — places we do not control and cannot inspect in advance. That is the defining feature of safety in this practice, and this policy is written around it rather than around an office we mostly do not use.

Health includes psychological health. Psychosocial hazards are managed on the same footing as physical ones.

2. WHO THIS APPLIES TO

Every worker: employees, casuals, contractors, labour hire and students on placement. It also shapes how we work with participants, families and other providers.

3. WHAT OPAL WILL DO

• Identify hazards and assess risks before work starts, including a documented risk screen for each new participant environment.
• Control risks using the hierarchy of control — eliminate first, and use personal protective equipment only when higher controls are not reasonably practicable.
• Provide the information, training, instruction and supervision needed to work safely, and provide it before you are exposed to the hazard rather than after.
• Provide and maintain safe equipment, including manual handling aids, and supply personal protective equipment at no cost to you.
• Consult workers on matters that affect their health and safety, and consult genuinely — that means before a decision, with enough information to form a view.
• Maintain first aid arrangements and emergency procedures.
• Record, investigate and act on incidents, injuries and near misses.
• Hold workers compensation insurance, and support recovery at work after an injury.
• Never treat a worker unfavourably for raising a safety concern, refusing genuinely unsafe work, or making a claim.

4. WHAT YOU MUST DO

Section 28 of the WHS Act places duties on you personally. While at work you must:
• take reasonable care for your own health and safety;
• take reasonable care that what you do, or fail to do, does not adversely affect others;
• comply with reasonable instructions on health and safety, so far as you are able; and
• co-operate with Opal's health and safety policies and procedures.

In practice that means:
• Complete your WHS induction before your first participant visit.
• Do a dynamic risk assessment on arrival at every environment — and leave if it is not safe. You will never be criticised for leaving.
• Follow the Home Visit and Lone Worker policies, including check-in and check-out.
• Use the manual handling techniques and equipment you have been trained in. Do not lift or transfer a person alone where the plan calls for two people or a hoist.
• Report hazards, incidents, near misses and injuries — the same day, and before the end of your shift for anything serious.
• Do not work impaired by alcohol, other drugs, medication side effects or fatigue.
• Tell us about a health condition or medication that could affect your safe performance of the work. This is treated confidentially and used to make adjustments, not to exclude you.

5. THE HAZARDS THAT ACTUALLY ARISE HERE

5.1 Driving. The largest single risk in a mobile role, and it grows with fatigue and rural distance. See the Vehicle and Travel Policy.

5.2 Unfamiliar and uncontrolled environments. Trip hazards, animals, hoarding, smoking indoors, unsafe electrical fittings, no clear exit, other people present who were not expected. See the Home Visit & Community Work Safety Policy.

5.3 Working alone. See the Lone Worker Policy.

5.4 Occupational violence and aggression. From participants, family members, or others present. Aggression is a hazard to be controlled, never something to be absorbed as part of the job.

5.5 Manual handling. Transfers, equipment trials, assistive technology, carrying assessment kits, and prolonged awkward postures during home assessments.

5.6 Infection. See the Infection Prevention and Control Policy.

5.7 Psychosocial hazards. Exposure to trauma and distressing content, high emotional demand, isolation from colleagues, unreasonable workload or time pressure, poor role clarity, bullying or harassment, and the cumulative weight of clinical responsibility. These are risks to be assessed and controlled, and the controls are real ones: caseload management, supervision, debriefing after a difficult event, and the ability to say a workload is not safe.

5.8 Remote and rural work. Distance from help, poor mobile coverage, long single-day drives, and weather. See the Emergency and Disaster Management Policy.

6. RAISING A CONCERN

Tell your supervisor first, in most cases. Anything you would rather not raise there goes to [TO CONFIRM: the named WHS contact and their contact details].

If you reasonably believe that carrying out work would expose you to a serious risk from an immediate or imminent hazard, you may cease that work. Tell Opal as soon as you can and stay available for other suitable work. This right sits in the WHS Act and using it will not count against you.

You may also contact WorkSafe WA on 1300 307 877 at any time.

7. CONSULTATION

Health and safety is a standing item at [TO CONFIRM: the meeting where WHS is discussed, and how often]. Opal's health and safety representative arrangements are: [TO CONFIRM: HSR arrangements, or record that no HSR has been requested]. Any worker may ask for an HSR to be elected.

8. TRAINING

Before starting participant-facing work: WHS induction, manual handling, infection control, and the home visit and lone worker procedures. Refreshed at [TO CONFIRM: refresher frequency]. First aid: [TO CONFIRM: which roles require a current first aid certificate, and who holds one].

title: Equal Opportunity, Anti-Discrimination & Respectful Workplace Policy
summary: Opal Therapy's commitment to a workplace free of discrimination — the protected attributes, what discrimination looks like in recruitment and at work, the duty to make reasonable adjustments, and how to raise a concern.
body:
EQUAL OPPORTUNITY, ANTI-DISCRIMINATION & RESPECTFUL WORKPLACE POLICY

1. PURPOSE AND COMMITMENT

Opal Therapy makes employment decisions on merit — the skills, experience and qualities a role actually needs — and on nothing else. This applies to recruitment, pay, hours, allocation of work, training, promotion, discipline and termination.

It is not only a legal obligation. A disability service that does not itself employ, adjust for and promote people with disability is not credible to the people it supports.

2. PROTECTED ATTRIBUTES

It is unlawful to discriminate against a person because of: sex; gender identity; sexual orientation; intersex status; marital or relationship status; pregnancy, potential pregnancy or breastfeeding; family responsibilities or carer status; race, colour, descent, national or ethnic origin, and Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander identity; religious or political conviction; age; disability, including a past, future or imputed disability, and an assistance animal; impairment; and having made a complaint about any of the above.

3. WHAT DISCRIMINATION LOOKS LIKE

3.1 Direct — treating someone less favourably because of a protected attribute. Not shortlisting an applicant because of their accent, assuming an older worker will not learn a new system, giving the interesting work to the person who is not a parent.

3.2 Indirect — a rule that applies to everyone but disadvantages a group, and that cannot be justified as reasonable. Requiring all staff at a 7:30am meeting that carers cannot attend, when the meeting could be at 9:00.

3.3 In recruitment. Advertising, screening, interviewing and referee checks are all covered. Do not ask about pregnancy plans, marital status, age, religion, health or disability except where you are asking whether a person can perform the inherent requirements of the role, with adjustments.

4. REASONABLE ADJUSTMENTS

Opal will make reasonable adjustments so that a person with disability can apply for, perform and progress in a role, unless doing so would impose unjustifiable hardship. Adjustments are usually small and cheap: modified hours, a different chair, screen-reading software, additional breaks, adjusted duties during recovery, a quieter workspace, flexible location, more written instructions.

Ask for one by contacting [TO CONFIRM: who to contact to request a workplace adjustment]. You do not have to disclose a diagnosis to request an adjustment, and information you do give is kept confidential and used only to arrange it. An adjustment request is a normal operational conversation, not a performance matter.

5. RESPECTFUL WORKPLACE

Beyond the law, this is about what daily life here feels like. Use people's correct names and pronouns. Do not make jokes at the expense of a group. Do not comment on someone's body, accent, food, religion or family arrangements. Include people in conversations and decisions that affect them. Assume good faith when you disagree, and take the disagreement to the person rather than around them.

If you get it wrong — a wrong pronoun, an assumption that landed badly — correct it, briefly, and move on. Over-apologising makes it about you.

6. RECRUITMENT AND SELECTION

Selection criteria are based on the inherent requirements of the role and set before applications are read. Interview questions are the same for every candidate. Panels avoid single-person decisions where possible. Reasons for decisions are recorded. Anyone with a personal relationship to a candidate declares it and steps out of the decision, under the Conflict of Interest Policy.

7. PARTICIPANTS AND FAMILIES

The same standard applies to how we treat participants and how we allow our workers to be treated. A request to change worker because of a worker's race, sex, religion, disability or sexuality is not accommodated as a matter of preference. A request grounded in a genuine cultural or trauma-related need — for example a participant requesting a clinician of the same sex for personal care — is a different matter and is considered on its merits, with the reasoning recorded.

8. RAISING A CONCERN

Speak to your supervisor, or to [TO CONFIRM: the named contact for discrimination complaints]. The process, the protections against victimisation, and the external avenues are the same as in the Bullying, Harassment & Sexual Harassment Policy, including the WA Equal Opportunity Commission, the Australian Human Rights Commission and the Fair Work Commission.

You may raise a concern about something you witnessed, not only something done to you.

9. BREACHES

Discrimination and vilification are disciplinary matters up to and including dismissal, and may expose both Opal and the individual to legal liability.

title: Participant Rights, Choice and Control
summary: The rights every person we support holds — dignity, privacy, choice, communication, advocacy, freedom from restrictive practice — and the specific things a worker must do to make each of them real rather than stated.
body:
PARTICIPANT RIGHTS, CHOICE AND CONTROL

1. PURPOSE

Every person we support holds these rights already. Nothing in this document grants them. What it does is state what a worker has to actually do so that a right the person already has is not quietly unavailable in practice.

2. THE RIGHTS, AND WHAT THEY REQUIRE OF YOU

2.1 To be treated with dignity and respect
Speak to adults as adults, whatever their disability or communication method. Never use a childish tone, a nickname they have not chosen, or baby talk. Do not talk about a person over their head to a carer while they are in the room. Knock, wait, and ask before entering a bedroom or bathroom. Do not touch a person, their mobility aid or their belongings without asking — a wheelchair is part of someone's body space, not furniture.

2.2 To make their own decisions
Assume capacity. Capacity is decision-specific and can vary with the day, the topic and how well the information was explained. If a person appears not to understand, the first question is whether we explained it in a form they can use.
Offer genuine options, including doing nothing. Explain the trade-offs honestly. Accept a decision you disagree with, and record the recommendation, the discussion, and the person's decision.
Supported decision-making comes before substitute decision-making. Where a guardian or nominee is formally appointed, work with them and still include the participant in the conversation about their own life.

2.3 To communicate in their own way
Interpreters, Auslan, AAC devices, communication boards, plain language, Easy Read, extra time, written follow-up. Arranged and paid for by Opal, not by the participant.
The obligation is on us to be understood, and to understand. If a session is not working, the communication method is the first thing to change.

2.4 To privacy and confidentiality
See the Privacy & Confidentiality Policy. In their home, that also means practical things: not reading documents left out, not opening cupboards you have not been invited into, not discussing them with a neighbour who asks.

2.5 To have a support person or advocate
Anyone may bring a family member, friend or advocate to any appointment. Independent advocacy contacts are offered on request, and we will help someone find one. Never suggest that involving an advocate will make things harder.

2.6 To complain, and to be listened to
Every participant is told how to complain, in a form they can use, at the start of the service and again whenever it is relevant. That includes the external bodies in the Complaints Management Policy. Never imply that complaining could affect the supports someone receives.

2.7 To be free from violence, abuse, neglect, exploitation and discrimination
See the Safeguarding Policy. Discrimination on the basis of race, sex, age, sexuality, gender identity, religion, or any other protected attribute has no place in how we deliver a service.

2.8 To be free from unauthorised restrictive practice
A restrictive practice is anything that restricts the rights or freedom of movement of a person — including physical, mechanical, chemical and environmental restraint, and seclusion. Restrictive practices are only ever used where they are authorised, are part of a behaviour support plan, and are the least restrictive option available.
Where a recommendation you make would have a restrictive effect — a lock, a bed rail, a seat belt on a chair, a restrictive door handle — that is a restrictive practice question, not just an equipment question. Raise it with your supervisor before recommending it.

2.9 To choose and change their provider
A participant may decline a support, ask for a different clinician, or leave Opal, without giving a reason and without any consequence for how they are treated in the meantime. Transfer their records promptly when they ask, and do not make leaving difficult.

2.10 To take risks
Dignity of risk is a right. Adults are entitled to make choices that carry risk, including choices we would advise against. Our job is to make sure the decision is informed, to record the conversation and the person's decision, and to reduce the risk in the way they have agreed to — not to remove the choice.

3. WHERE IT USUALLY GOES WRONG

Not by anybody deciding to override a right. It goes wrong through habit and time pressure: assuming the carer speaks for the participant because it is quicker; explaining once, in clinical language, and treating a nod as agreement; recommending the safest option rather than the one the person wants; not offering an interpreter because the family member present can translate; scheduling a visit at a time that suits the roster.

4. IF YOU SEE A RIGHT BEING DENIED

Whether by a family member, a support worker, another provider, or an Opal colleague, raise it. Document what you observed. Where it involves abuse, neglect or an unauthorised restrictive practice, report it immediately under the Safeguarding and Incident Management policies.

title: Social Media Policy
summary: How to use social media without putting a participant's privacy, your registration or Opal Therapy's reputation at risk — covering personal accounts, Opal's accounts, participant connection requests, and the advertising rules that bind registered health practitioners.
body:
SOCIAL MEDIA POLICY

1. PURPOSE

Nothing in this policy is about stopping you having a life online. It is about three specific risks: a participant being identifiable when you did not intend it, a registered practitioner breaching the National Law's advertising rules, and Opal being represented by someone who was not speaking for it.

The National Law's advertising provisions apply to a registered practitioner's social media the same way they apply to a billboard. AHPRA has been explicit that the same obligations apply online as offline, including to content on a personal account.

2. THE RULE THAT COVERS MOST SITUATIONS

Assume everything you post is permanent, public, and will be read by a participant, their family, your regulator and a future employer. Privacy settings are a preference, not a protection.

3. PARTICIPANTS

3.1 Never post about a participant. Not their name, not their photo, not their story, not a "de-identified" anecdote. De-identification is much harder than it feels: in a small practice, in a small town, the combination of a suburb, a diagnosis, an age and a date is often enough. A participant recognising themselves in your post has had their privacy breached whether or not anyone else recognises them.

3.2 Never post a photo taken in a participant's home, a school, or any setting where a participant might be identifiable — including a photo of equipment, a modification, a view, or your own coffee on their table.

3.3 Do not accept or send friend or follow requests to participants or their family members on personal accounts. If a request arrives, do not accept it, and tell the participant kindly at the next session why not — that it is a rule about keeping the relationship professional, not a judgement about them.

3.4 If a participant contacts you through a personal account, do not respond substantively. Redirect them to Opal's contact channels and record it.

3.5 Do not look up participants on social media. Where there is a genuine clinical or safety reason to, discuss it with your supervisor first and document the reason.

4. PERSONAL ACCOUNTS

4.1 You are free to have opinions and to express them. You are not free to identify yourself as an Opal clinician while doing something that damages Opal's participants, colleagues or reputation.

4.2 Where your profile identifies your profession or employer, add a line to the effect that views are your own.

4.3 Do not post anything that discriminates against, harasses or vilifies any person or group. The Bullying and EEO policies apply to what you post as much as to what you say in a car park.

4.4 Do not post about colleagues, internal disagreements, employment matters or Opal's clients, contracts or systems.

4.5 Do not post photographs of Opal premises, screens, or documents. A screenshot with a portal window in the background has disclosed more than you meant it to.

5. IF YOU ARE A REGISTERED PRACTITIONER

The National Law's advertising provisions apply to anything you post that promotes a regulated health service, including on a personal account. In particular:
• Testimonials about a clinical service must not be used in advertising. Do not solicit them, and do not share, repost or "like" one in a way that turns it into your advertising. Where you control a page, remove a testimonial posted by someone else.
• Do not make claims that are false, misleading or deceptive, or that create an unreasonable expectation of benefit.
• Do not offer a gift, discount or inducement without stating its terms.
• Do not use titles or claims of expertise you do not hold.

If you are unsure whether something you want to post counts as advertising a regulated health service, ask before posting.

6. OPAL'S OWN ACCOUNTS

6.1 Only people authorised by [TO CONFIRM: who is authorised to post on Opal's social media accounts] post on Opal's behalf.

6.2 Every post about a participant, including a photograph, requires written, specific, informed consent obtained in advance, recorded in the participant's file, and revocable. Consent to one post is not consent to reuse.

6.3 Comments on Opal's accounts are moderated. Anything raising a complaint or a clinical concern is taken offline and handled under the Complaints Management Policy — never argued with in public, and never answered with information about the person.

7. IF SOMETHING GOES WRONG

If you post something you should not have, take it down and tell your supervisor immediately. Deletion does not undo it, and telling someone quickly is what allows Opal to handle it — including notifying the participant if their privacy has been affected, which we would have to do under the Privacy & Confidentiality Policy.

If you see content that puts a participant's privacy at risk — posted by a colleague, a family member or anyone else — report it.

title: Safeguarding — Violence, Abuse, Neglect and Exploitation Policy
summary: How Opal Therapy prevents, recognises and responds to violence, abuse, neglect, exploitation and sexual misconduct against the people we support — including what you must do the moment you suspect it.
body:
SAFEGUARDING — VIOLENCE, ABUSE, NEGLECT AND EXPLOITATION POLICY

1. PURPOSE AND POSITION

People with disability experience violence, abuse, neglect and exploitation at far higher rates than the general population, and it is most often committed by someone they know and depend on. Opal's position is unqualified: we do not tolerate it, we do not manage it internally to protect a reputation, and we report it.

This policy applies whether the person causing harm is an Opal worker, a family member, another provider, a support worker, another participant, or a stranger.

2. WHAT WE ARE TALKING ABOUT

• Physical abuse — hitting, rough handling, unauthorised restraint, over-medication.
• Sexual abuse and sexual misconduct — any sexual act without consent, any sexual contact with a person who cannot consent, grooming, exposure to sexual material, and any sexualised behaviour toward a participant by a worker.
• Emotional and psychological abuse — threats, humiliation, intimidation, isolation, controlling who a person sees.
• Neglect — failing to provide food, shelter, hygiene, medical care, supervision or supports the person depends on, including by omission.
• Financial abuse and exploitation — taking or misusing money or property, pressuring a person over money, misuse of a debit card or NDIS funds, unpaid work.
• Systemic and service abuse — inflexible routines that strip choice, withholding a support as punishment, restrictive practices used without authorisation.

3. PREVENTION

3.1 Screening. Everyone in a participant-facing role holds the checks their role requires, verified before they start and kept current. Working with Children Check requirements are determined by the actual duties of the role, not by job title, and Opal will tell you in writing which checks apply to you.

3.2 Supervision and visibility. Lone work with a participant is normal in this profession, so the safeguard is documentation and supervision rather than a second person in the room. Sessions are recorded in the clinical record, plans are shared with the participant, and supervision is a place to raise unease early.

3.3 Boundaries. The Professional Boundaries Policy is a safeguarding control, not an etiquette guide. Most serious harm begins with a boundary that was crossed quietly and never mentioned.

3.4 Participant voice. Participants are told, in a format they can understand, that they can say no, that they can complain, and who to complain to. A participant who knows how to raise something is the strongest safeguard in the system.

4. RECOGNISING IT

Take seriously: unexplained or inconsistently explained injuries; fear of a particular person; sudden withdrawal, regression or distress; sexualised behaviour or knowledge that does not fit the person; poor hygiene or unmet basic needs where support is funded; missing money or possessions; a carer who will not leave the person alone with you; a participant's own disclosure, however partial.

None of these proves abuse. All of them require you to act under section 5. You are not being asked to investigate or to decide. You are being asked to report what you observed.

5. WHAT TO DO — IMMEDIATELY

5.1 Make the person safe. Call 000 if they are in immediate danger or need urgent medical care.

5.2 If a participant discloses to you:
• Listen. Do not interrupt, do not correct them, and do not ask leading or probing questions — a well-meant question can compromise a later investigation.
• Believe them and say so, in words like "thank you for telling me, I believe you, that should not have happened."
• Do not promise to keep it secret. Say clearly that you have to tell someone whose job it is to help keep them safe.
• Write down what they said in their own words, as close to verbatim as you can, as soon as you can, with the date and time.

5.3 Preserve evidence. Do not clean, tidy, wash clothing, or move things where a criminal offence may have occurred.

5.4 Report. Immediately by phone to [TO CONFIRM: the named safeguarding contact and their number], and to [TO CONFIRM: the after-hours safeguarding contact and their number] out of hours. Then record it as an incident in the portal within 24 hours under the Incident Management Policy.

5.5 Do not confront the alleged perpetrator, do not warn them, and do not tell colleagues who do not need to know.

6. EXTERNAL REPORTING

6.1 Police. Any suspected criminal offence — assault, sexual offence, theft, fraud — is reported to police. This is not a decision for Opal to weigh against other considerations.

6.2 Children. Concerns about a child's safety are reported to the Department of Communities Child Protection and Family Support (WA), Central Intake on 1800 273 889, or 000 in an emergency.
Occupational therapists are not among the professions listed as mandatory reporters under section 124B of the Children and Community Services Act 2004 (WA). Opal nevertheless requires every worker to report a child protection concern, as a condition of working here. If you hold another registration or role that does make you a mandatory reporter, that legal duty applies to you personally and is not displaced by anything in this policy.

6.3 NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission. 1800 035 544. Where Opal is a registered NDIS provider, the reportable incidents regime imposes statutory notification duties and timeframes — see the Incident Management Policy. Any person, at any time, may make a complaint to the Commission directly, and no worker may be discouraged from doing so.

6.4 AHPRA. Where the concern is about a registered health practitioner, a notification may be required under the National Law.

7. IF THE CONCERN IS ABOUT AN OPAL WORKER

They will be removed from contact with the participant while the matter is assessed. Suspension in these circumstances is a neutral protective step and is not a finding. The matter is reported externally as section 6 requires, whether or not the internal process has concluded, and Opal will not attempt to resolve an allegation of abuse "internally" as an alternative to reporting it.

8. NO DETRIMENT, AND NO SILENCE

Nobody will be disadvantaged for reporting a safeguarding concern in good faith, even if it turns out to be unfounded. Failing to report a concern is a serious disciplinary matter and may be a breach of the NDIS Code of Conduct.

Nothing in any Opal contract, agreement or settlement prevents a person from reporting abuse to police, to a regulator, or to a court.

9. RELATED DOCUMENTS

summary: How Opal Therapy works day to day — the practice, the people, the systems, the rhythms of the week, and where to go when something goes wrong. The handbook explains; the policies bind.
body:
WELCOME TO OPAL THERAPY — EMPLOYEE HANDBOOK

HOW TO USE THIS HANDBOOK

This handbook explains how the practice works. It is not a contract and it does not create entitlements. Where it summarises a policy, the policy itself is the authority and is in the portal's document library in full. Where it summarises your contract or an award, those win.

1. ABOUT OPAL THERAPY

Opal Therapy Pty Ltd, trading as Opal Therapy, ABN 51 824 753 556.
Office: 1 Baylis Street, Wagga Wagga NSW 2650 · Phone 02 6931 0000 · hello@opaltherapy.com.au · [TO CONFIRM: website]
NDIS provider status: [TO CONFIRM: registered, unregistered, or registration in progress — this determines several obligations referenced in the policies]

We are an occupational therapy practice working mainly with NDIS participants, delivering assessment, therapy, assistive technology, home modification and functional capacity work, largely in participants' own environments and including regional and rural visits.

2. OUR VALUES, IN THE FORM THEY ACTUALLY TAKE

The participant decides. Our expertise informs a decision that is not ours to make. If a participant declines a recommendation, that is a legitimate outcome and it gets documented as one.

Do the unglamorous part properly. Reports, notes, follow-up calls, chasing a supplier. Most of the value a participant receives is delivered by somebody being organised on their behalf.

Say it early. Concerns, mistakes, doubts about a plan, doubts about your own capacity this week. Every serious problem this practice has had began as a small one someone chose not to mention.

Small practice, real standards. Being small is not a reason for informal record-keeping, vague scope or ad-hoc safety.

3. TEAM STRUCTURE AND KEY PEOPLE

[TO CONFIRM: the practice structure — who reports to whom, and what each role covers]

Key contacts:
• Your supervisor: [TO CONFIRM: assigned per employee — shown on your onboarding record in the portal]
• Practice manager / operations: [TO CONFIRM: name and contact]
• Clinical lead: [TO CONFIRM: name and contact]
• Payroll and HR queries: [TO CONFIRM: name and contact]
• WHS contact: [TO CONFIRM: name and contact]
• Privacy contact: privacy@opaltherapy.com.au
• Complaints contact: complaints@opaltherapy.com.au
• After-hours contact, for safety matters only: [TO CONFIRM: name and number]

4. HOW WE WORK

4.1 The shape of a week. Most clinical days are a mix of participant visits, travel between them, and documentation time. Documentation time is scheduled, not squeezed into the gaps — if it is disappearing, that is a caseload problem to raise in supervision rather than an evening to absorb.

4.2 Caseload. Allocated by your supervisor with regard to complexity, travel and your experience. Caseload is reviewed in supervision. You are expected to say when it is not sustainable, and that conversation will not be held against you.

4.3 Participant-centred practice. Goals come from the participant, in their words, and are written that way in the plan. Sessions start by checking what has changed since last time. Recommendations are explained in a form the person can actually use — plain language, visual, translated, or via their support person. Where a participant has a decision-maker, we work with the decision-maker without talking past the participant.

4.4 Scope. Work within your training, your registration and your supervision. Referring on, or asking for a joint visit, is the right call more often than new graduates expect.

5. COMMUNICATION

5.1 With participants. Respond to a participant contact within [TO CONFIRM: expected response time]. If you cannot answer yet, say so and say when. Phone a participant if you are running late — a text is not enough when someone has arranged their day around you.

5.2 Within the team. [TO CONFIRM: which channel is used for what — email, portal messaging, phone, team chat]. Clinical decisions are recorded in the clinical record, not left in a chat thread.

5.3 Meetings. [TO CONFIRM: the regular meeting rhythm — team meeting, clinical review, WHS discussion, and how often each occurs]

5.4 Tone. Everything you write may be read later by the participant, their family, a funder, a regulator or a court. Write accordingly, and write about people the way you would want to be written about.

6. HOURS, LEAVE AND PAY

6.1 Hours. Your ordinary hours are in your contract. Record your time accurately in the portal, including payable travel.

6.2 Leave. See the Leave and Attendance Policy. Request planned leave early; call in as early as you can when you are unwell, so appointments can be moved rather than cancelled.

6.3 Payroll. Paid [TO CONFIRM: pay cycle and pay day] by electronic transfer. Pay slips are issued within one working day of payday. Superannuation is paid to your nominated fund, or to a stapled fund identified through the ATO if you have not nominated one. Check your first pay slip carefully and raise anything that looks wrong immediately — a payroll error caught in week one is a correction, and the same error caught in month six is a reconciliation.

7. TRAVEL, RURAL VISITS AND EXPENSES

7.1 Travel is a large part of this job. Plan routes to reduce driving, build in breaks, and do not schedule a full clinical day on top of a long drive. See the Vehicle and Travel Policy.

7.2 Rural and regional visits. Plan these in advance with your supervisor: overnight arrangements, mobile coverage, fuel, fatigue, and a check-in schedule that someone is actually watching. Do not depart on a remote visit without a check-in plan. See the Lone Worker Policy and the Emergency and Disaster Management Policy.

7.3 Expenses. Pre-approve anything unusual, keep receipts, claim in the portal. See the Expenses and Reimbursement Policy.

8. SYSTEMS

8.1 The portal is the system of record for participants, scheduling, clinical documentation, onboarding, policies, resources and compliance. If it is not in the portal, it did not happen and cannot be evidenced.

8.2 Email and calendar. Use your Opal account for all work. Keep your calendar accurate and up to date — colleagues rely on it to know where you are, which is a safety control as well as a scheduling one.

8.3 AI-assisted features. Some portal features use AI assistance under governance controls, including a kill switch and audit logging. AI output is a draft for you to check and take responsibility for, never a substitute for your clinical judgement, and never something to be sent onward unread. Do not paste participant information into any AI tool that is not part of the portal.

8.4 Security. Multi-factor authentication where offered, locked screens, no participant information in personal accounts or on personal devices. See the Information Security & Acceptable Use Policy.

9. CLINICAL DOCUMENTATION

Notes are written the same day wherever possible, and the standard is set out in the Clinical Documentation Policy. In short: contemporaneous, factual, legible to a stranger, distinguishing what you observed from what you concluded, and never altered silently. Reports are checked before they go out — by you, and by your supervisor where the policy requires it.

10. SUPERVISION AND PROFESSIONAL DEVELOPMENT

Supervision is scheduled, protected and not the first thing cancelled when a week gets busy. It is for clinical reasoning, caseload, professional development and the things that are bothering you, and it is a place where saying "I got this wrong" is safe.

CPD: the Occupational Therapy Board requires at least 20 hours per registration year, including a minimum of five hours in an interactive setting. You are responsible for meeting it and for keeping your own evidence. See the Supervision, Performance and CPD Policy for what Opal contributes.

11. SAFETY

Read the Work Health and Safety Policy before your first participant visit, along with the home visit, lone worker and infection control policies.

The three things that matter most in this role: assess the environment on arrival every single time; leave if it is not safe, and never apologise for that; and check in and out as the lone worker procedure requires, so somebody notices if you do not.

12. WHEN SOMETHING GOES WRONG

12.1 Immediate danger. Call 000.

12.2 Incidents, injuries, near misses. Tell your supervisor the same day and log it in the portal within 24 hours. See the Incident Management Policy.

12.3 Safeguarding concerns. Report immediately under the Safeguarding Policy — you do not need to be sure, and you are not being asked to investigate.

12.4 Complaints. Any concern raised by a participant or family member is a complaint. Take it, record it, pass it on the same day, and never discourage it. See the Complaints Management Policy.

12.5 Something about your own work. Tell your supervisor early. Errors reported promptly are handled as learning; errors discovered later are handled differently.

13. EMERGENCY CONTACTS

Emergency services: 000
Poisons Information Centre: 13 11 26
Health Direct: 1800 022 222
Opal after-hours safety contact: [TO CONFIRM: name and number]
NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission: 1800 035 544
WorkSafe WA: 1300 307 877
[TO CONFIRM: employee assistance programme contact, or a note that none is currently provided]

14. WHEN YOU LEAVE

Give the notice your contract requires, hand over your caseload properly, return equipment and keys, and remember that your confidentiality obligations do not end with your employment. We will provide a statement of service on request, and we would rather you left well than quietly.

EXPENSES AND REIMBURSEMENT POLICY

1. PRINCIPLE

If you have to spend your own money to do your job, Opal pays it back. You should not be out of pocket for work, and you should not be waiting months to be made whole.

The other side of that: spend Opal's money as if it were your own, and get approval before spending it on anything unusual.

2. WHAT IS REIMBURSED

2.1 Travel. Work-related vehicle use under the Vehicle and Travel Policy, at [TO CONFIRM: the rate per kilometre or method]. Parking at a participant visit. Public transport for work travel. Tolls.

2.2 Overnight travel. Accommodation and meals for approved regional or rural work, within [TO CONFIRM: accommodation and meal limits per night]. Book through [TO CONFIRM: how accommodation is booked, and whether it is paid directly by Opal].

2.3 Professional. Registration and CPD costs to the extent covered by the Supervision, Performance and CPD Policy. Professional association membership: [TO CONFIRM: whether membership is reimbursed and up to what value]. Approved courses and conferences, including reasonable travel.

2.4 Clinical materials and equipment. Assessment tools, consumables and therapy materials, with prior approval above [TO CONFIRM: approval threshold].

2.5 Phone and internet. [TO CONFIRM: whether Opal provides a phone, or pays an allowance or a proportion of a personal plan].

2.6 Working with Children Check, NDIS Worker Screening Check and police check fees where the role requires them: [TO CONFIRM: which screening costs Opal pays, and whether it pays upfront or reimburses].

2.7 Personal protective equipment and infection control supplies are provided by Opal at no cost to you. Under work health and safety law these are not a cost that may be passed to a worker, and you should not be buying them yourself. If you have had to, claim it and tell your supervisor that the supply failed.

3. WHAT IS NOT REIMBURSED

• Parking and traffic fines, and any other penalty.
• Personal travel, including home to your usual place of work.
• Alcohol.
• Personal items, clothing other than approved uniform or PPE, and grooming.
• Costs incurred without required prior approval, unless approved afterwards on genuinely exceptional grounds.
• Anything you cannot substantiate with a receipt or a tax invoice.
• A gift or hospitality you provided to a participant or a referrer — see the Gifts and Benefits Policy.

4. APPROVAL

4.1 Anything over [TO CONFIRM: pre-approval threshold] needs written approval before you spend it.

4.2 Anything unusual needs approval regardless of value. If you are wondering whether it needs approval, it does.

title: Infection Prevention and Control Policy
summary: Standard precautions for occupational therapy delivered in homes, schools and community settings — hand hygiene, PPE, equipment cleaning, what to do when you or a participant is unwell, and how to respond to a blood or body fluid exposure.
body:
INFECTION PREVENTION AND CONTROL POLICY

1. PURPOSE

We move between households in a single day, and many of the people we see are more vulnerable to infection and less able to recover from it than the general population. The risk this policy manages is not only to you — it is that you become the connection between one home and the next.

2. STANDARD PRECAUTIONS

Standard precautions apply to every participant, every time, regardless of their known infection status. They are not reserved for people known to be infectious, because you often will not know.

2.1 Hand hygiene. The single most effective control. Clean your hands:
• before entering a participant's home or space, and immediately on leaving;
• before and after any contact with a participant;
• before and after putting on and removing gloves;
• after contact with body fluids, equipment or surfaces;
• before eating and after using the toilet.
Soap and running water for at least 20 seconds where hands are visibly soiled, and after contact with vomit or diarrhoea. Alcohol-based hand rub otherwise. Carry your own — do not assume a home will have either.

2.2 Personal protective equipment. Supplied by Opal at no cost to you. Gloves for contact with body fluids, broken skin or contaminated surfaces. A mask where a respiratory illness is present or where a participant is immunocompromised. Eye protection where splashing is possible. An apron or gown for procedures likely to soil clothing.
PPE is removed and disposed of before you leave, and hand hygiene follows removal. Never wear the same gloves between two participants, and never wear gloves as a substitute for hand hygiene.

2.3 Respiratory hygiene. Cover a cough with your elbow or a tissue, dispose of the tissue immediately, and clean your hands.

2.4 Sharps and body fluids. Do not recap needles. Use a sharps container where sharps are involved. Treat all blood and body fluids as potentially infectious.

3. EQUIPMENT AND VEHICLES

3.1 Clean assessment equipment between participants — goniometers, dynamometers, pens, tablets, test kits, and anything a participant handled.

3.2 Equipment loaned to a participant is cleaned and, where required, disinfected before it goes out and after it comes back. Record it.

3.3 Keep clean and used items separated in your car. Carry hand rub, gloves, wipes and a small waste bag as standard.

3.4 Clean your phone and tablet daily. They go everywhere with you and get cleaned less than anything else you carry.

4. WHEN YOU ARE UNWELL

4.1 Do not attend a participant with symptoms of an infectious illness — fever, a new or worsening cough, sore throat, vomiting or diarrhoea. Call in under the Leave and Attendance Policy.

4.2 Stay away until you meet the current exclusion period for the illness, and at least 24 hours after vomiting or diarrhoea has resolved. Where a public health direction applies, it takes precedence over this policy.

4.3 Do not attend while symptomatic because a participant would otherwise miss a session. Reschedule. Nobody at Opal will be criticised for that decision.

5. WHEN A PARTICIPANT OR HOUSEHOLD IS UNWELL

Screen before you go — a phone call the morning of a visit is enough. Where someone in the household is unwell, consider rescheduling, switching to telehealth, or attending with additional precautions. Discuss it with your supervisor rather than deciding alone under time pressure, and record the decision.

Some participants are immunocompromised and are scheduled deliberately — [TO CONFIRM: whether higher-risk participants are scheduled first in the day, and how they are identified].

6. IMMUNISATION

Opal recommends that clinical staff maintain immunisations recommended for healthcare workers, including an annual influenza vaccination. Where a specific immunisation is a requirement for a role or a setting — a school, a hospital or a residential facility may impose one — you will be told in writing before you start that work.
Opal's position on which immunisations are required rather than recommended, and any support offered: [TO CONFIRM: required immunisations by role, and whether Opal funds them].
Immunisation information is health information and is handled under the Privacy & Confidentiality Policy.

7. EXPOSURE TO BLOOD OR BODY FLUIDS

Act immediately, in this order:
1. Wash the area with soap and water. Do not scrub. For an eye or mouth splash, rinse with water or saline.
2. Seek medical assessment urgently — an emergency department or your GP, the same day. Post-exposure prophylaxis is time-critical and its effectiveness falls with delay.
3. Tell your supervisor immediately and report it as an incident within 24 hours.
4. Follow the Injury Management System information for workers — this may be a workers compensation matter.

Do not wait until the end of the day to seek assessment, and do not decide on your own that the exposure was probably not significant.

8. AN OUTBREAK OR A PUBLIC HEALTH DIRECTION

Opal follows WA Department of Health and Commonwealth directions, which override this policy while they are in force. Additional measures may include screening, masks, testing, changed service delivery, or a temporary move to telehealth. You will be told what applies and for how long. See the Emergency and Disaster Management Policy.

9. TRAINING

Infection control is part of the WHS induction, before your first participant visit, and is refreshed at [TO CONFIRM: refresher frequency].

title: Clinical Documentation Policy
summary: The standard for clinical records at Opal Therapy — what goes in a note, when it must be written, how errors are corrected, what must never be altered, and how AI-assisted drafting is governed.
body:
CLINICAL DOCUMENTATION POLICY

1. PURPOSE

A clinical record has four jobs: it keeps the participant's care coherent across time and across clinicians; it evidences that the support was delivered; it is the primary source if a decision is ever questioned; and it is the participant's own account of their therapy, which they are entitled to read.

A record written only for the first of those is not good enough for the other three.

2. WHO THIS APPLIES TO

Everyone who records anything about a participant — clinicians, students on placement, and administrative staff recording contacts and correspondence.

3. WHEN TO WRITE

3.1 Contemporaneously. Write the note during or immediately after the contact. Where that is genuinely not possible, write it the same working day, and in any event within 24 hours.

3.2 A late note is written honestly. It records the date of the contact and the date it was written, and it does not pretend to be contemporaneous. A note that misstates when it was made damages the credibility of every other note in the file.

3.3 Never write a note in advance of the contact it describes.

4. WHAT EVERY ENTRY CONTAINS

• Participant identifier, date, start and finish times, and the setting.
• Who was present, including family, carers, support workers and interpreters.
• The purpose of the contact and what was actually done.
• Objective observations, and measurements where they were taken.
• The participant's own words for anything significant, in quotation marks.
• Your clinical reasoning — why you did what you did, and what you considered and ruled out.
• Any risk identified and what you did about it.
• What was agreed, what the participant chose, and anything they declined.
• The plan, with who is doing what by when.
• Your full name, role and signature or authenticated portal entry.

5. HOW TO WRITE IT

5.1 Separate observation from interpretation. "Participant sat on the edge of the bed for 40 seconds before standing" is an observation. "Participant is deconditioned" is an interpretation. Both belong, but not in the same sentence pretending to be one thing.

5.2 Write for a stranger. Assume the reader is a therapist who has never met this person, reading in two years, under time pressure. Expand abbreviations that are not universally understood.

5.3 Write for the participant. They can ask to read it. Avoid loaded language — "non-compliant", "attention-seeking", "difficult", "refused" — where a factual description does the job better. "Declined the recommended rail and explained that she does not want a hospital-looking bathroom" is more useful clinically and more respectful than "non-compliant".

5.4 Record what did not happen too. A cancelled session, an unanswered call, a recommendation declined, a referral not yet actioned. Gaps in a record are read as gaps in care.

5.5 Third parties. Record information about family members and others only where it is relevant to the participant's care, and remember they may see it.

6. CORRECTIONS AND AMENDMENTS

6.1 Never delete, overwrite or backdate. Never use correction fluid on paper or edit an entry to say something different from what was recorded.

6.2 Correct by amendment. Add a new dated, signed entry that states what was wrong and what the correct position is. The original stays visible. The portal enforces this; on paper, strike through with a single line so the original remains legible, and initial and date the change.

6.3 A participant may ask for a correction. See the Privacy & Confidentiality Policy. The same rule applies: their disagreement is recorded alongside the original, not instead of it.

7. REPORTS AND CORRESPONDENCE

7.1 Reports must be accurate, within your scope, and clear about the limits of the assessment — what was and was not assessed, in what setting, over what period, and what the findings do not support.

7.2 Do not write a recommendation you do not clinically support because a funder, a family member or a coordinator wants it. Funding pressure is exactly the situation this rule exists for.

7.3 Reports going to a funder, a tribunal or another provider are reviewed before they are sent, in line with [TO CONFIRM: which reports require supervisor review before release].

7.4 Give the participant a copy of any report about them unless there is a documented reason not to.

8. AI-ASSISTED DOCUMENTATION

Opal's portal includes AI-assisted drafting under governance controls, including audit logging and a kill switch. The rules are simple and non-negotiable:
• AI output is a draft. You read every line, you correct it, and you own what you sign.
• Never sign a note you have not read in full.
• Do not paste participant information into any AI tool that is not part of the portal.
• Where a recording or transcript is used to help produce a note, the participant's consent is obtained first and recorded, and the retention of that recording follows the Records Management Policy.
• If AI-generated text asserts something that did not happen, that is a clinical record error — correct it under section 6 and report it, because it tells us something about the tool.

9. ACCESS, STORAGE AND RETENTION

Records are stored in the portal, not on local drives, personal devices or personal cloud accounts. Retention is governed by the Records Management Policy: at least seven years from the last contact for an adult, and for a child, at least until they turn 25.

10. WHAT GOES WRONG MOST OFTEN

Notes written days later from memory. Sessions documented as planned rather than as they happened. Risk noticed but not written down. A phone call with a family member that never reached the file. A report sent without a supervisor check. Each of these is recoverable if you say so; none of them is recoverable if the first time anyone hears about it is at a coronial inquest or a tribunal.
