title: Lone Worker Policy
summary: The check-in and escalation system that makes sure somebody notices if you do not come back — who monitors it, what happens when a check-in is missed, and the extra arrangements for remote and rural work.
body:
LONE WORKER POLICY

1. PURPOSE

Almost everyone here works alone for most of the day. The specific risk this policy addresses is not that something happens — it is that something happens and nobody knows for hours.

The WHS Regulations require an employer to provide a system of work that includes effective communication with a worker carrying out remote or isolated work. This is that system. It only works if it is used every time, including on the ordinary days, because a check-in system that is used selectively cannot tell the difference between a missed check-in and a forgotten one.

2. WHO IS A LONE WORKER HERE

Anyone working without another Opal worker present: a home visit, a school or community visit, travel between appointments, work in the office outside normal hours, and any remote or rural visit.

3. THE CHECK-IN SYSTEM

3.1 Your calendar is the baseline. Every visit is in it, with the address and the expected finish time, kept current during the day. A colleague must be able to answer "where is she right now?" from your calendar alone.

3.2 Check in and out for each visit by [TO CONFIRM: the check-in method — portal, SMS to a monitored number, or a phone call — and the number or channel].

3.3 Who monitors it: [TO CONFIRM: the role that monitors check-ins during business hours, and after hours].

3.4 Extend it if you are running over. A visit that runs long is normal; an unannounced visit that runs long is indistinguishable from a problem.

4. ESCALATION WHEN A CHECK-IN IS MISSED

This is what happens if you do not check out, and it is the reason the system matters:

Step 1 — after [TO CONFIRM: minutes] past the expected finish, the monitor phones you.
Step 2 — no answer: they phone again and send a message, and try [TO CONFIRM: any secondary contact method].
Step 3 — still no answer after [TO CONFIRM: minutes]: they phone the participant or the site on the number in the file.
Step 4 — still unresolved: they notify [TO CONFIRM: the escalation contact] and attempt to locate you, including your emergency contact.
Step 5 — where there is reason to believe you are at risk, they call the police on 131 444, or 000 if there is immediate concern.

Opal will always err toward escalating. If a missed check-in turns out to be a flat battery, that is a good outcome, not an embarrassment, and nobody will be criticised for triggering it.

5. YOUR OBLIGATIONS

• Check in and check out, every time.
• Keep your calendar accurate.
• Keep your phone charged, on, and on you — not in your bag in the car.
• Answer or return a check-in call promptly.
• Tell the monitor before you go somewhere with poor coverage, and give an expected clear time.
• Update the monitor if plans change during the day.
• Do not disable location sharing where it forms part of the arrangement.

6. DURESS AND CODE WORDS

Where you need help but cannot say so in front of someone, use the agreed duress phrase: [TO CONFIRM: the agreed duress word or phrase, and who is trained to recognise it]. It should be something you could say in a normal call — for example asking about a file or a person that does not exist. Anyone receiving it escalates immediately to step 5 and does not ask a clarifying question.

Personal duress alarms: [TO CONFIRM: whether duress alarms or a lone worker app are provided, and to whom].

7. REMOTE AND RURAL WORK

7.1 Plan it in advance with your supervisor. A remote visit is not a normal visit that happens to be further away.

7.2 Before departure, agree: the route, the expected arrival and return times, overnight arrangements, coverage blackspots and clear times, fuel stops, and who is monitoring.

7.3 Where there is no reliable mobile coverage, a satellite messenger or a personal locator beacon is required: [TO CONFIRM: what remote communication equipment Opal provides and how it is booked].

7.4 Carry water, food, a first aid kit and warm clothing appropriate to the season. See the Vehicle and Travel Policy for the vehicle requirements.

7.5 Fatigue is the dominant risk on a long rural day. Do not plan a full clinical load on top of a long drive, and do not drive home after a day that has already run long — see the Vehicle and Travel Policy for overnight arrangements.

8. AFTER HOURS AND OFFICE WORK ALONE

Tell someone if you are working alone in the office outside normal hours, lock the external doors, and check in when you leave. The same escalation applies.

9. IF THE SYSTEM FAILS

If you cannot reach the monitor, if a check-in was missed and nobody followed up, or if the arrangement is not workable in practice, report it as a WHS matter. A control that quietly stopped working is more dangerous than no control at all, because everyone is relying on it.

title: Incident Management Policy
summary: What counts as an incident, how to report one, the timeframes that apply, and which incidents must be notified to WorkSafe WA or the NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission.
body:
INCIDENT MANAGEMENT POLICY

1. PURPOSE

An incident management system does two things: it makes sure the person harmed is looked after, and it makes sure the same thing is less likely to happen to the next person. Both depend on incidents actually being reported, which is why this policy is written to make reporting easy and safe rather than to make it rare.

2. WHAT IS AN INCIDENT

An incident is any act, omission, event or circumstance that:
• caused harm, or could reasonably have caused harm, to a participant, a worker, or anyone else in connection with our work; or
• involves alleged violence, abuse, neglect, exploitation or discriminatory conduct; or
• involves the use of a restrictive practice that was not authorised or not in a behaviour support plan; or
• is a near miss — something that did not cause harm this time only because of luck or a late intervention.

Near misses are reported on the same form as everything else. A near miss is the cheapest possible warning and treating it as "nothing happened" is how a practice discovers a hazard the expensive way.

3. WHAT TO DO, IN ORDER

3.1 Make everyone safe. Give or arrange first aid. Call 000 if anyone is seriously hurt or at immediate risk. Remove the hazard if it is safe to do so.

3.2 Do not disturb the scene of a serious incident. Where someone has died, been seriously injured, or a dangerous incident has occurred, the site must be left undisturbed until WorkSafe WA says otherwise, except to help an injured person, remove a body, make the site safe, or act under police direction.

3.3 Tell someone the same day. Notify your supervisor immediately by phone for anything serious, and in any event before the end of your shift. Serious means: an injury needing more than basic first aid, an allegation of abuse, a death, a police or ambulance attendance, a missing participant, a medication error, or anything you would want to be told about if it were your family member.

3.4 Record it in the portal within 24 hours. Report what happened, not what you think should have happened. Include the date, time and location, who was involved and who witnessed it, what you observed in factual terms, what you did, who you notified, and the participant's own account in their own words wherever they can give one.

3.5 Keep the record honest. Do not speculate about cause, do not assign blame, and do not amend an earlier note to make the sequence look tidier. If your understanding changes, add a new dated entry.

4. NOTIFICATIONS TO REGULATORS

You are not expected to make these notifications yourself. Your job is to escalate fast enough that the person who does can meet the deadline.

4.1 WorkSafe WA. Under the Work Health and Safety Act 2020 (WA), a notifiable incident — the death of a person, a serious injury or illness, or a dangerous incident — must be notified to WorkSafe WA immediately after becoming aware of it, with written notification to follow. Records of a notifiable incident must be kept for at least five years.

4.2 NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission. The reportable incidents regime under the NDIS Act binds registered NDIS providers. Opal's current registration status is recorded in the portal's onboarding settings; where Opal is a registered provider, reportable incidents — including death, serious injury, abuse or neglect, unlawful sexual or physical contact, sexual misconduct, and the unauthorised use of a restrictive practice — must be notified to the Commission within the statutory timeframe, which is 24 hours for most categories and five business days for an unauthorised restrictive practice.
Where Opal is not a registered provider, that notification duty does not apply to us, and every other step in this policy still does. Opal's own escalation is not conditional on registration status.

4.3 Police. Call the police for any suspected criminal conduct, including assault, sexual offences, theft and fraud. Do not let an internal process delay a police report.

4.4 Other. A mandatory notification about a registered health practitioner goes to AHPRA. A privacy breach follows the Privacy & Confidentiality Policy. A workers compensation injury follows the Injury Management System information for workers.

5. WHAT HAPPENS NEXT

5.1 Support first. The participant and their family or nominee are told what happened, in plain language, and what we are doing about it. Workers involved in a serious incident are offered support, including [TO CONFIRM: employee assistance programme details, or state that none is currently provided].

5.2 Review. Every incident is reviewed by [TO CONFIRM: role responsible for incident review]. Serious incidents get a documented review that asks what in the system allowed this, not who to blame. Findings that change practice are fed back to the team.

5.3 Records. Incident records are retained for at least seven years, and longer where a regulator requires it.

6. NO DETRIMENT

Nobody at Opal will be disadvantaged for reporting an incident in good faith, including one they caused. Failing to report is the disciplinary matter.

7. RELATED DOCUMENTS

Safeguarding — Violence, Abuse, Neglect and Exploitation Policy · Complaints Management Policy · Work Health and Safety Policy · Injury Management System — information for workers · Clinical Documentation Policy

title: Complaints Management Policy
summary: How a participant, family member, worker or member of the public can complain about Opal Therapy, what we do with a complaint, and the external bodies a person can go to instead of or as well as us.
body:
COMPLAINTS MANAGEMENT POLICY

1. PURPOSE

A complaint is information we would not otherwise have. This policy makes it easy to give us that information, and it commits us to responding to it without the person paying a price for having spoken up.

2. WHO CAN COMPLAIN, AND ABOUT WHAT

Anyone. A participant, a family member, a carer, a nominee, an advocate, a worker, another provider, or a member of the public. About anything — the quality of a support, the behaviour of a worker, a decision we made, a bill, an appointment, the way we handled an earlier complaint.

A person may complain anonymously. An anonymous complaint is recorded and acted on; we simply cannot report an outcome back.

3. HOW A COMPLAINT REACHES US

• In person or by phone to any worker.
• To complaints@opaltherapy.com.au.
• By phone on 02 6931 0000 or by email to hello@opaltherapy.com.au.
• Through a support person, advocate or interpreter — and we will help arrange one, at no cost, if that is what a person needs to be able to complain.

4. YOUR OBLIGATIONS AS A WORKER

4.1 Take it. If someone raises a concern with you, that is a complaint, whether or not they use the word. Do not tell them to put it in writing first and do not require them to use a form.

4.2 Listen before you explain. Let the person finish. Do not defend Opal, your colleague or yourself in the moment.

4.3 Never discourage a complaint, and never suggest that making one could affect the supports a participant receives. That suggestion is itself a serious breach of the NDIS Code of Conduct.

4.4 Record and pass it on the same day. Log it in the portal and tell complaints@opaltherapy.com.au, even if you have already resolved it on the spot — a resolved complaint is still a data point.

4.5 If the complaint is about you, hand it over. Pass it to your supervisor or to [TO CONFIRM: the alternative complaints contact where the complaint concerns the usual contact]. Do not investigate a complaint about your own conduct.

4.6 Tell the person what happens next, in the words of section 5 below.

5. WHAT WE COMMIT TO

• Acknowledge every complaint within [TO CONFIRM: acknowledgement timeframe, commonly 2 business days].
• Tell the person who is handling it and how to contact them.
• Keep them informed while it is open, at least every [TO CONFIRM: update interval].
• Aim to resolve it within [TO CONFIRM: resolution target, commonly 21 or 28 days], and explain the delay if we cannot.
• Give the outcome, the reasons, and what we are changing as a result.
• Explain how to escalate if they are not satisfied, including to the bodies in section 7.
• Deal with the complaint fairly, confidentially, and without cost to the complainant.

6. NO DETRIMENT

No participant will receive a lesser service because they complained. No worker will be disadvantaged for making a complaint or for supporting someone else's. Any suggestion of retaliation is treated as a serious matter in its own right.

7. GOING OUTSIDE OPAL

A person does not have to complain to us first, and can go to any of these at any time:

• NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission — 1800 035 544, ndiscommission.gov.au
• AHPRA, for a concern about a registered practitioner — 1300 419 495, ahpra.gov.au
• Health and Disability Services Complaints Office (WA) — 1800 813 583, hadsco.wa.gov.au
• Office of the Australian Information Commissioner, for a privacy concern — 1300 363 992, oaic.gov.au
• Fair Work Ombudsman, for an employment concern — 13 13 94, fairwork.gov.au
• Police, for anything that may be a crime — 000 in an emergency, 131 444 otherwise

These contact details must be given to any participant who asks how to complain, and must not be withheld or delayed.

8. WHAT WE DO WITH THE PATTERN

Complaints are reviewed together, at least [TO CONFIRM: review frequency for complaint trends], by [TO CONFIRM: role responsible]. One complaint is an event; three of the same complaint is a system problem, and it is the second reading that changes how we work.

9. RECORDS

Complaint records are kept for at least seven years, separately from the participant's clinical record, so that a complaint never sits in a file in a way that could colour someone's clinical care.

title: Opal Therapy Code of Conduct
summary: The standard of behaviour Opal Therapy expects of everyone who works here, built on the seven elements of the NDIS Code of Conduct and the shared Code of conduct that applies to registered occupational therapists.
body:
OPAL THERAPY CODE OF CONDUCT

1. PURPOSE

This Code sets out how everyone at Opal Therapy is expected to behave. It exists because the people we work with are often relying on us at a point in their lives when they have limited ability to walk away from a service that treats them badly. That imbalance is the reason a code of conduct is not optional paperwork.

This Code does not replace your professional obligations. If you are a registered occupational therapist, the Occupational Therapy Board of Australia's Code of conduct applies to you in full, and where that Code sets a higher standard than this one, the higher standard wins. The same is true of the NDIS Code of Conduct, which applies to workers delivering NDIS supports whether or not the provider is registered.

2. WHO THIS APPLIES TO

Everyone. Employees, casual staff, contractors, students on placement, and anyone else delivering work on Opal's behalf. It applies during work, and it applies outside work where your conduct affects a participant, a colleague, or the trust the public places in the practice.

3. THE SEVEN THINGS THE NDIS CODE OF CONDUCT REQUIRES

These are the NDIS Code's own elements. Opal adopts them without modification and everything else in this document explains how we expect them to be met day to day.

3.1 Act with respect for individual rights to freedom of expression, self-determination and decision-making, in accordance with applicable laws and conventions.
3.2 Respect the privacy of people with disability.
3.3 Provide supports and services in a safe and competent manner with care and skill.
3.4 Act with integrity, honesty and transparency.
3.5 Promptly take steps to raise and act on concerns about matters that may impact the quality and safety of supports and services.
3.6 Take all reasonable steps to prevent and respond to all forms of violence against, and exploitation, neglect and abuse of, people with disability.
3.7 Take all reasonable steps to prevent and respond to sexual misconduct.

4. WHAT THIS LOOKS LIKE IN PRACTICE

4.1 Respect and choice

• Assume capacity. A participant's right to make a decision does not depend on you agreeing with the decision.
• Where a participant has a decision-maker, guardian or nominee, work with them without talking past the participant.
• Offer real options, including the option of declining a support, and record what was chosen.
• Use the participant's preferred name, pronouns and communication method. If you do not know them, ask.
• Adjust how you communicate to the person in front of you — interpreters, Auslan, plain language, AAC, extra time. The obligation to be understood is ours, not theirs.

4.2 Safety and competence

• Work within your scope of practice, your training and your supervision arrangements. Saying "this is outside what I can safely do" is a professional strength, not an admission.
• Prepare. Read the file before the session, not during it.
• Do not practise when impaired — by illness, fatigue, alcohol, other drugs, or a health condition that affects your judgement. Tell your supervisor instead.
• Keep your registration, insurance, screening checks and mandatory training current. The portal will remind you; the obligation is still yours.

4.3 Integrity and honesty

• Claim only for supports actually delivered, for the time actually taken, at the agreed rate.
• Do not overstate what a support can achieve, and do not let a funding conversation shape a clinical recommendation.
• Correct your own errors promptly and in writing. Amending a record honestly is safe here; concealing an error is not.
• Declare conflicts of interest as they arise, under the Conflict of Interest Policy.

4.4 Speaking up

• If you see or suspect harm, poor practice or a risk to a participant, you must raise it. This is element 3.5 of the NDIS Code and it is not discretionary.
• Report to your supervisor or to [TO CONFIRM: the named person for conduct concerns and their contact details]. If the concern is about that person, report to [TO CONFIRM: the alternative escalation contact].
• You can also report directly to a regulator — the NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission, AHPRA, WorkSafe WA, or the police — and nothing in this Code and no instruction from anyone at Opal may discourage you from doing so.
• Opal will not tolerate detriment of any kind against a person who raises a concern honestly. Retaliation is itself a breach of this Code.

4.5 Preventing violence, abuse, neglect, exploitation and sexual misconduct

• Never use physical force, threats, humiliation, or the withdrawal of a support as a way to manage behaviour.
• Restrictive practices are only ever used where they are authorised, documented, and consistent with a behaviour support plan. If you are ever unsure whether something is a restrictive practice, treat it as one and ask.
• Sexual or intimate contact with a participant is prohibited, without exception, including where a participant appears to consent or initiates it.
• Report suspected abuse or neglect immediately under the Safeguarding Policy, whether or not the alleged perpetrator works for Opal.

5. BREACHES

A breach of this Code is a disciplinary matter and may also be a matter for a regulator or the police. Opal will investigate proportionately and fairly, tell you what is alleged, give you a real chance to respond, and keep the process confidential so far as it can. Outcomes range from additional supervision through to termination and notification to AHPRA or the NDIS Commission.

Reporting your own mistake early will always be treated more favourably than the same mistake discovered later.

6. RELATED DOCUMENTS

Professional Boundaries Policy · Safeguarding — Violence, Abuse, Neglect and Exploitation Policy · Incident Management Policy · Complaints Management Policy · Conflict of Interest Policy · Social Media Policy · Privacy & Confidentiality Policy

7. QUESTIONS

Ask your supervisor. If your question is about whether something is allowed, ask before you do it — that conversation is always cheaper than the alternative.

title: Supervision, Performance and CPD Policy
summary: How clinical supervision works at Opal Therapy, what performance conversations look like, and the continuing professional development and recency requirements that keep an occupational therapist registered.
body:
SUPERVISION, PERFORMANCE AND CPD POLICY

1. PURPOSE

Supervision is a clinical safety control, not a management ritual. In a practice where clinicians work alone in other people's homes most of the day, it is the main mechanism by which a problem gets noticed by someone other than the person having it.

2. SUPERVISION

2.1 Everyone in a clinical role has a named supervisor, identified in the portal.

2.2 Frequency. New graduates and staff new to a practice area: [TO CONFIRM: frequency for new graduates, commonly weekly for the first three months]. Experienced clinicians: [TO CONFIRM: ongoing frequency, commonly fortnightly or monthly]. Additional sessions are available on request, and asking for one is not a signal of difficulty.

2.3 Protected time. Supervision is scheduled and is not the first thing cancelled when a week is busy. If it is repeatedly rescheduled, escalate that — the pattern is the problem, not the individual session.

2.4 What it is for. Clinical reasoning and case discussion; complex, risky or stuck cases; ethical and boundary questions; caseload and workload; professional development; and how you are actually going. All of it.

2.5 What is recorded. A brief record of the date, the cases and issues discussed, decisions and actions agreed, and anything to follow up. Clinical decisions made in supervision are also recorded in the participant's file. Personal matters you raise are not recorded in detail.

2.6 Confidentiality and its limits. What you discuss stays between you unless it involves a risk to a participant or a worker, a reportable incident, unsafe practice, or something a regulator must be told. Your supervisor will tell you when a limit applies.

2.7 Bring the difficult thing. Supervision is worth what you put into it. A supervisor who only hears about the cases that are going well is unable to help with the ones that are not.

2.8 External supervision. Where specialist expertise is needed — [TO CONFIRM: which practice areas require external supervision, and Opal's contribution to its cost].

3. PERFORMANCE

3.1 Ongoing feedback rather than an annual surprise. Anything raised at a review should already have been said.

3.2 Formal review at [TO CONFIRM: review cycle, commonly at three months and then annually]. It covers achievements, goals, development, workload, and what Opal needs to do differently.

3.3 Underperformance is addressed openly, early, and with support: a clear statement of the concern, what is expected, what help is available, and a reasonable period to demonstrate change. You may bring a support person to any formal performance meeting.

3.4 Serious misconduct is handled under the relevant conduct policy, not as a performance matter.

3.5 Nothing in this policy limits your rights under your contract, an award or the Fair Work Act.

4. CONTINUING PROFESSIONAL DEVELOPMENT

4.1 The Occupational Therapy Board's registration standard requires at least 20 hours of CPD per registration year, including a minimum of 5 hours in an interactive setting with other practitioners. That is the current standard; the Board can revise it, and the portal holds the figures Opal is currently applying.

4.2 CPD must be relevant to your practice, and you must keep your own evidence — a CPD portfolio with dates, activities, hours, and a reflection on what changed in your practice. AHPRA audits it, and the obligation is personal.

4.3 What counts: courses and workshops, supervision and peer review, journal reading with reflection, presenting or teaching, research, professional reading, and mentoring. What does not: attendance without any record or reflection.

4.4 Opal's contribution: [TO CONFIRM: paid CPD days, financial contribution per year, and the approval process].

4.5 Mandatory training Opal requires regardless of CPD: [TO CONFIRM: list of mandatory training and refresher intervals].

5. RECENCY OF PRACTICE AND REGISTRATION

5.1 The Board's recency of practice standard requires a minimum amount of practice over a defined period. The figures Opal currently applies are held in the portal's onboarding settings, and the standard itself is the authority.

5.2 Registration renews annually by 30 November. Renewing on time is your responsibility. Practising while unregistered is an offence under the National Law, and Opal cannot roster you to clinical work without current registration.

5.3 Tell Opal immediately if a condition, undertaking, caution or reprimand is placed on your registration, if you are the subject of a notification, or if your registration lapses.

5.4 Professional indemnity insurance arrangements must be in place for your whole scope of practice. Opal's arrangements: [TO CONFIRM: whether Opal's professional indemnity insurance covers employees, the insurer, and what it does and does not cover].

6. STUDENTS AND NEW GRADUATES

Students are supervised at a level appropriate to their stage, and the supervising clinician remains responsible for the participant's care and for the clinical record. New graduates receive additional supervision, a graduated caseload, and joint visits until their supervisor agrees they are ready to work independently.

7. WHEN YOU ARE STRUGGLING

Say so. Not being confident with a case, a technique or a caseload is normal and is a supervision matter, not a performance one. Where your health is affecting your ability to practise safely, tell your supervisor early — there are adjustments available, and the National Law obligations that apply to an impaired practitioner are much better met before someone is harmed.

title: Telehealth Policy
summary: When telehealth is clinically appropriate and when it is not, consent, the platform and privacy requirements, how to run a safe session including an emergency plan, and how telehealth is documented and claimed.
body:
TELEHEALTH POLICY

1. PURPOSE

Telehealth is how a great deal of rural and regional occupational therapy becomes possible at all. It is also easy to deliver badly, and the failure modes — a missed environmental hazard, a participant who cannot use the platform, an emergency you cannot reach — are specific enough to be planned for.

The professional standards that apply in person apply identically by video. Scope of practice, consent, documentation, privacy and boundaries do not change with the medium.

2. WHEN TELEHEALTH IS APPROPRIATE

Well suited to: review and follow-up, coaching and education, goal setting and planning, some functional interviews, equipment training and troubleshooting, report feedback, family and team meetings, and maintaining continuity when travel is not possible.

Not appropriate, or only with an in-person component, where: hands-on assessment or physical measurement is required; a home or workplace environment must be assessed properly; pressure care, seating or complex equipment prescription is involved; a participant cannot engage with the format even with support; there are safeguarding concerns that need eyes in the room; or there is significant risk that could not be managed remotely.

A first appointment is normally in person. Where it is not, record why.

3. THE DECISION IS CLINICAL

Choose telehealth because it suits the participant and the clinical task, not because it suits the schedule. Where the participant would prefer in person and it is reasonably possible, do it in person. Record the reason for the mode in the clinical record.

Reassess it. A support that started well by video can stop working; if a participant is disengaging, the format is one of the first things to change.

4. CONSENT

Before the first telehealth session, explain and record consent covering: what telehealth involves and its limitations; that they can decline or switch to in person at any time without any effect on their supports; who else will be present at each end; how privacy is protected; what happens if the technology fails; and what happens in an emergency.
Consent is recorded in the file and is revocable at any time.

Sessions are not recorded unless there is a specific purpose, separate written consent, and a defined retention period under the Records Management Policy. Never record covertly. Ask participants not to record without telling you, and if they say they are recording, that is their choice to make about their own care — note it in the record.

5. PLATFORM AND PRIVACY

5.1 Use the approved platform: [TO CONFIRM: the approved telehealth platform and where the meeting is created]. Do not move a session to a personal video account, a social media call or a consumer messaging app.

5.2 Your end. A private room with the door closed. Nobody else in earshot, including at home. Headphones. A neutral background with no participant information, no screens, no whiteboards and no files visible. Close everything on your screen you would not want shared, before you share anything.

5.3 Their end. Ask at the start who else is present and who can hear. A participant may not be able to speak freely, and that matters most in exactly the situations where it is least visible. If you have any concern that someone is present who should not be, change the subject and follow it up separately.

5.4 Confirm identity at the start of the first session, and be alert to the possibility that you are speaking to someone other than the person you booked.

6. BEFORE THE SESSION

• Confirm the participant can use the platform, and offer a test call before the first session.
• Ask what support they need — a support person, an interpreter, a larger screen, a phone call as a fallback.
• Confirm their physical location for this session, and their phone number. Do this every time, not just the first time. If you cannot say where they are, you cannot send help.
• Confirm an emergency contact and, where relevant, local emergency services for their location — which will not be yours on a regional call.
• Send any materials in advance.

7. DURING THE SESSION

Start by confirming location, who is present, and what to do if the connection drops — agree that you will phone them, so nobody sits waiting.

Work more slowly than in person. Check understanding more often. Watch for fatigue, which arrives sooner on video, and offer breaks.

Be honest about what you cannot see. If an assessment needs something you cannot observe properly, say so and arrange it in person rather than recording a conclusion the medium did not support.

8. IF SOMETHING GOES WRONG

Connection drops: phone them, as agreed. If you cannot reach them and there was any concern, escalate — emergency contact, then emergency services for their location.

A medical or safety emergency during a session: call 000 and give their address, which is why section 6 requires you to have it. Stay on the line with them if you can. Follow the Emergency and Disaster Management Policy and report it as an incident.

A safeguarding disclosure by video is handled exactly as one in person, under the Safeguarding Policy.

9. DOCUMENTATION AND CLAIMING

Record the mode of delivery, the platform, the participant's location, who was present at both ends, the duration, and any limitation the format imposed on the assessment or the session.

Claim telehealth in line with the applicable NDIS pricing arrangements and the participant's service agreement. Do not claim travel that did not occur.

title: Records Management Policy
summary: What Opal Therapy keeps, where it keeps it, how long for, how it is destroyed, and the rules that apply when a record is subject to a subpoena, a complaint or an investigation.
body:
RECORDS MANAGEMENT POLICY

1. PURPOSE

Two failures are possible with records, and they pull in opposite directions: keeping something too long, and not being able to produce something you should still have. This policy sets out which is which.

2. SCOPE

Every record Opal creates or receives, in any format — portal entries, documents, email, photographs, recordings, text messages about work, handwritten notes, and paper files.

A work-related message on a personal device is an Opal record. That is a reason to keep work communication on Opal systems, where it is captured properly.

3. THE SYSTEM OF RECORD

The portal is the system of record. A record that exists only in your email, on a local drive, in a notebook or on a personal device is not filed, cannot be found by anyone else, and cannot be produced when it is needed.

Working documents are moved into the portal when they are finished. Personal drives and desktops are not storage.

4. RETENTION PERIODS

These are minimum periods. Where two apply, the longer one wins.

4.1 Adult participant clinical records — at least 7 years from the date of last contact.

4.2 Child or young person's clinical records — until the person turns 25, or 7 years from last contact, whichever is later. The reason is the limitation period: it generally does not begin to run until a person turns 18.

4.3 Employee records — at least 7 years after employment ends, as the Fair Work Act requires for time and wages records.

4.4 Workplace injury, workers compensation and rehabilitation records — [TO CONFIRM: retention period, noting exposure-related records may need to be kept far longer].

4.5 WHS records — hazard, incident and risk records for at least 5 years, and longer for a notifiable incident or where exposure monitoring applies.

4.6 Incident and complaint records — at least 7 years.

4.7 Financial and tax records — at least 5 years, and 7 where another obligation applies.

4.8 Recordings, photographs and video — kept only for the purpose and period the participant consented to, and destroyed at the end of it. Consent is recorded with the file.

4.9 Unsuccessful job applications — [TO CONFIRM: retention period for unsuccessful applicants].

5. DESTRUCTION

5.1 Nothing is destroyed except under an approved schedule, and the destruction is recorded — what, when, by whom, under what authority.

5.2 Paper is destroyed by secure shredding or a secure destruction service. Electronic records are deleted from live systems and from backups in line with the backup cycle. Devices are securely wiped or physically destroyed before disposal.

5.3 Never destroy a record on your own initiative. If you think something should go, say so; do not act.

6. LEGAL HOLD — THE RULE THAT OVERRIDES EVERYTHING ABOVE

The moment a record is, or may become, relevant to a complaint, an incident investigation, a regulator's inquiry, a coronial matter, a subpoena, a claim or litigation:
• stop any scheduled destruction of it immediately;
• do not edit, tidy, reorganise or "complete" it;
• tell [TO CONFIRM: role responsible for legal holds] straight away.

Altering or destroying a record that is subject to a legal process is a criminal offence, and doing it out of a wish to be helpful is not a defence. Preserve first, ask second.

7. REQUESTS FOR RECORDS

7.1 A participant asking for their own records — Privacy & Confidentiality Policy. Do not release anything yourself.

7.2 A subpoena, warrant, court order or statutory notice — pass it to [TO CONFIRM: role responsible for handling subpoenas] the day it arrives. Deadlines are short and non-negotiable.

7.3 Another provider requesting records — only with the participant's consent, or where a lawful exception applies.

7.4 A transfer of care — provide records promptly when a participant moves to another provider. Opal keeps its copy for the retention period; the participant leaving does not shorten it.

8. QUALITY

A record you cannot find is a record you do not have. Name things consistently, file them where they belong, and file them promptly. Version control matters most on documents that go out — the version sent to a funder must be identifiable later.

9. BACKUPS AND CONTINUITY

Opal's systems are backed up under [TO CONFIRM: backup arrangement and restore testing frequency]. Backups are not an archive: they exist to recover from failure, not to satisfy retention obligations.

body:
LEAVE AND ATTENDANCE POLICY

1. PURPOSE

What leave you get, how to ask for it, and what to do when something goes wrong on a workday. Your contract and any applicable award or industrial instrument sit above this policy; where they differ, they win, and this policy is never the source of a lesser entitlement than the law provides.

2. AN IMPORTANT CAVEAT ABOUT ENTITLEMENTS

Which set of minimum entitlements applies to you depends on whether Opal is a national system employer under the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) or a Western Australian state system employer. An incorporated entity trading in WA is normally in the national system; a sole trader or unincorporated partnership normally sits in the WA state system, where the Minimum Conditions of Employment Act 1993 (WA) applies instead of the National Employment Standards.

Opal's position: [TO CONFIRM: whether Opal is a national system or WA state system employer, and the applicable award or industrial instrument].

The figures in section 3 state the National Employment Standards. If Opal is a WA state system employer, the WA equivalents apply and this policy must be amended before it is published. Long service leave in WA is governed by the Long Service Leave Act 1958 (WA) in either case.

3. LEAVE ENTITLEMENTS

3.1 Annual leave. Four weeks paid annual leave per year for full-time employees, accruing progressively and pro-rata for part-time employees. Casual employees do not accrue annual leave; casual loading is paid instead.

3.2 Personal/carer's leave. Ten days paid personal/carer's leave per year for full-time employees, pro-rata for part-time, accruing progressively and carrying over. Use it when you are unfit for work because of illness or injury, or to care for a member of your immediate family or household who is ill, injured or affected by an unexpected emergency. Casual employees are entitled to two days unpaid carer's leave per occasion.

3.3 Compassionate leave. Two days per occasion, paid for permanent employees and unpaid for casuals, when a member of your immediate family or household dies or suffers a life-threatening illness or injury, and also in the case of a miscarriage or stillbirth.

3.4 Family and domestic violence leave. Ten days paid leave in a 12-month period, available in full from the first day, to every employee including casuals, and renewing each year rather than accruing. It does not need to be taken in one block.
This is treated with particular care. Information about it is kept confidential and is not recorded on a pay slip in a way that identifies it. If you need it, contact [TO CONFIRM: the confidential contact for family and domestic violence leave] directly — you do not have to go through your supervisor.

3.5 Parental leave. Up to 12 months unpaid parental leave after 12 months continuous service, with the right to request a further 12 months. Government-funded Parental Leave Pay is administered by Services Australia and is separate from anything Opal pays. Opal's own paid parental leave position: [TO CONFIRM: whether Opal offers paid parental leave, and on what terms].

3.6 Long service leave. In Western Australia, 8⅔ weeks of paid long service leave after 10 years of continuous employment with the same employer, with a pro-rata entitlement on termination in defined circumstances after 7 years, under the Long Service Leave Act 1958 (WA).

3.7 Public holidays. You are entitled to be absent on a WA public holiday. Opal may reasonably request work on a public holiday and you may reasonably refuse.

3.8 Community service leave. Unpaid leave for a voluntary emergency management activity, and up to 10 days paid for jury service, in line with the National Employment Standards.

3.9 Study, conference and professional development leave. Covered in the Supervision, Performance and CPD Policy. Opal's allowance: [TO CONFIRM: paid CPD days and study leave per year].

4. REQUESTING LEAVE

4.1 Planned leave. Request it in the portal, as far ahead as you can, and at least [TO CONFIRM: notice period for planned leave] for a period longer than [TO CONFIRM: threshold, e.g. three days]. Approval considers participant continuity, other approved leave, and the size of the team on that day. Do not book flights before your leave is approved.

4.2 We will answer a leave request within [TO CONFIRM: response time], and we will not unreasonably refuse annual leave.

4.3 Unplanned absence. Call — do not text or email — [TO CONFIRM: who to call when you cannot work, and the number] as early as you can and by [TO CONFIRM: cut-off time, e.g. 8:00am] at the latest. Tell us whether you expect to be back tomorrow, so your appointments can be moved rather than cancelled.

4.4 Evidence. Medical evidence or a statutory declaration may be required for personal/carer's leave, and normally is for [TO CONFIRM: when evidence is required, e.g. absences of two or more consecutive days, or a day adjoining a public holiday]. A certificate never has to disclose your diagnosis.

5. YOUR PARTICIPANTS COME FIRST WHEN YOU ARE AWAY

You are not expected to work while on leave. You are expected to hand over: before planned leave, make sure notes are current, urgent matters are flagged to a colleague, reports due during your absence are either finished or reassigned, and your out-of-office and voicemail are set. For unplanned absence, Opal Therapy handles the handover — your only job is to tell us early enough that we can.

6. ATTENDANCE AND HOURS

6.1 Your ordinary hours are set out in your contract. Record your worked time accurately in the portal, including travel time where it is payable and any additional hours worked.

6.2 Timeliness matters more in this work than in most: a participant who has arranged their day, their transport and their support worker around a 10am appointment is materially harmed by a late arrival. If you are running late, phone the participant, not just the office.

6.3 Time in lieu, overtime and on-call arrangements: [TO CONFIRM: Opal's arrangements for overtime, time in lieu and any on-call expectation].

6.4 Flexible work. An employee in certain circumstances — including as a parent or carer, with a disability, aged 55 or over, or experiencing family and domestic violence — has a statutory right to request a flexible working arrangement, and Opal must respond in writing within 21 days and may only refuse on reasonable business grounds after genuinely discussing it with you.

7. UNAUTHORISED ABSENCE

Failing to attend without contact is treated seriously, both because of the participant impact and because we may not know you are safe. Repeated unexplained absence is a performance and conduct matter. If something in your life is making attendance difficult, tell us before it becomes that — there is almost always an adjustment available.

title: Privacy & Confidentiality Policy
summary: How Opal Therapy handles the personal, health and NDIS information of participants, employees and others — what we collect, who may see it, when we may disclose it without consent, and what a person can ask us for.
body:
PRIVACY & CONFIDENTIALITY POLICY

1. PURPOSE

Participants tell us things they have not told their family. They do it because they assume we will handle it properly. This policy says what "properly" means, so that assumption is a fact rather than a hope.

It covers information about participants, their families and carers, employees, contractors, job applicants and anyone else whose personal information reaches us.

2. THE INFORMATION WE HOLD

2.1 Participant information. Name and contact details, date of birth, NDIS number and plan details, diagnoses, assessment results, clinical notes, correspondence with other providers, funding and invoicing records, photographs or recordings where separately consented to, and information about family, carers and decision-makers.

2.2 Health information is sensitive information under the Privacy Act. It attracts a higher standard: as a general rule we need consent to collect it, and it may only be used for the purpose it was collected for, or a directly related purpose the person would reasonably expect.

2.3 Employee information. Recruitment records, identity and work-rights evidence, registration and screening checks, payroll and superannuation details, performance and supervision records, and health information where it is relevant to work capacity or an injury.

3. YOUR OBLIGATIONS AS A WORKER

3.1 Access on a need-to-know basis only. The portal's permission tiers are the floor, not the ceiling. Having technical access to a record is not authority to open it. Do not look up a participant you are not working with, a colleague, a friend, a family member, or yourself out of curiosity — every access is logged.

3.2 Never discuss a participant where you can be overheard. Not in a waiting room, a corridor, a lift, a car park, a cafe, or a shared house during a telehealth call.

3.3 Use Opal systems for Opal information. Do not move participant information into personal email, personal cloud storage, personal messaging apps or personal note-taking apps. If a tool you need is not available, ask for it rather than working around it.

3.4 Devices. Lock your screen when you step away. Keep devices encrypted and passcoded. Report a lost or stolen device immediately, and to [TO CONFIRM: after-hours contact for a lost device] if it is out of hours.

3.5 Paper. Keep it to a minimum, keep it out of sight in a vehicle or a home, return it the same day, and destroy it through secure disposal rather than a household bin.

3.6 Confidentiality outlasts employment. Your obligation continues after you leave Opal, indefinitely.

4. WHEN INFORMATION MAY BE SHARED

4.1 With the participant's consent. This is the normal path. Consent should be informed, specific about who and what, recorded in the file, and treated as revocable.

4.2 For the primary purpose of care. Sharing within the treating team so a participant receives coordinated support does not require a fresh consent each time, but it still requires the need-to-know test.

4.3 Without consent, where the law permits or requires it. This is a short list and each case must be recorded in the file and raised with your supervisor first wherever it is safe to do so:
• A serious and imminent threat to the life, health or safety of any person, or to public health or safety.
• A suspicion of child abuse or neglect, reported under the Safeguarding Policy.
• A reportable incident that must go to the NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission.
• A subpoena, warrant, court order or a statutory notice from a regulator.
• A mandatory notification about a health practitioner under the National Law.

4.4 When in doubt, do not disclose and ask. A disclosure cannot be undone. A delay of an hour to check almost always can be.

5. REQUESTS TO SEE OR CORRECT A RECORD

A person may ask for access to their own information, and may ask us to correct it. Do not answer a request like this on your own. Pass it to privacy@opaltherapy.com.au on the day you receive it. Opal will respond within [TO CONFIRM: response timeframe in days, 30 days is the common commitment], and if access is refused we will explain why in writing.

Correcting a clinical record does not mean deleting what was written. An error is corrected by an amendment that leaves the original visible and dated — a record that can be silently rewritten is worth nothing to the participant it is about.

6. THIRD PARTIES AND OVERSEAS STORAGE

Opal uses external providers to run its systems — cloud hosting, email, and AI-assisted features that operate under the portal's AI governance controls. These providers are bound by contract to protect the information and to use it only for the service they provide to us. Where information is stored or processed outside Australia, that is recorded in Opal's privacy collection notices. Current arrangements: [TO CONFIRM: list of external providers and the countries information is stored in].

7. BREACHES

Tell [TO CONFIRM: the person to notify of a suspected privacy breach] as soon as you suspect one — a misdirected email, a lost document, a record left open, an unauthorised access. Do not wait until you are certain, and do not attempt to fix it quietly first.

An eligible data breach under the Notifiable Data Breaches scheme must be assessed promptly and, where it is likely to cause serious harm, notified to the affected individuals and to the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner. That clock starts when someone becomes aware of the possibility, which is why reporting a suspicion matters more than reporting a conclusion.

Reporting a breach you caused will not, on its own, result in disciplinary action. Concealing one will.

8. RELATED DOCUMENTS

title: Vehicle and Travel Policy
summary: Driving for work at Opal Therapy — licence and insurance requirements, using your own car, fatigue on long rural drives, transporting participants and equipment, and what to do after a crash or a fine.
body:
VEHICLE AND TRAVEL POLICY

1. PURPOSE

Driving is the single largest physical risk in this practice. It is also the part of the job most likely to be treated as not really being work. Time in a vehicle is work time, a vehicle used for work is a workplace, and both are managed accordingly.

2. BEFORE YOU DRIVE FOR OPAL

2.1 Hold a current, unrestricted Australian driver licence appropriate to the vehicle, and give Opal a copy at onboarding and on renewal.

2.2 Tell Opal immediately if your licence is suspended, cancelled, restricted, or subject to conditions, or if you accumulate demerit points that put it at risk. Driving for work without a valid licence is not covered by insurance and is a serious disciplinary matter.

2.3 Tell Opal about any medical condition or medication that could affect your ability to drive safely.

3. USING YOUR OWN VEHICLE

3.1 Your vehicle must be roadworthy, currently registered, and comprehensively insured, with your insurer aware that it is used for work. Confirm this at onboarding and annually: [TO CONFIRM: how and when vehicle insurance and registration are verified].

3.2 Maintenance is yours — tyres, brakes, lights, wipers, fluids and servicing. Do not drive a vehicle you know is not roadworthy.

3.3 Reimbursement. Opal reimburses work-related travel at [TO CONFIRM: the rate per kilometre or the method used, and whether it follows the ATO rate]. Home to your usual place of work is not reimbursable; travel between participants, and to a participant directly from home where that is your first appointment, generally is. Record every trip in the portal on the day: date, purpose, start and finish points, and kilometres. See the Expenses and Reimbursement Policy.

3.4 Insurance excess after an at-fault crash while driving for work: [TO CONFIRM: whether Opal contributes to the excess, and in what circumstances].

4. OPAL VEHICLES

[TO CONFIRM: whether Opal provides pool vehicles. If it does, this section must cover booking, the pre-start check, fuel and toll cards, cleanliness, reporting damage, private use and who else may drive.]

5. DRIVING SAFELY

• Obey the road rules. A fine incurred while driving for work is yours to pay.
• No handheld phone use. Set navigation before you move off. Calls only through a properly mounted hands-free system, and pull over for anything that needs your attention.
• Do not write notes, read a file or eat while driving. Do not use the drive between appointments to catch up on documentation.
• Never drive under the influence of alcohol or drugs, including prescription medication that carries a driving warning.
• Wear a seatbelt, and make sure everyone in the vehicle does.
• Secure equipment. An unrestrained hoist, wheelchair or assessment kit becomes a projectile in a crash. Heavy items go in the boot or are strapped down.
• Adjust for conditions — rain, dust, glare, unsealed roads, and wildlife at dawn and dusk on country roads.

6. FATIGUE

6.1 Fatigue is the specific hazard of rural work in this state, and the distances are the reason. Treat it as a hazard to be planned around, not willpower to be applied.

6.2 Plan a break of at least 15 minutes every two hours of driving.

6.3 Maximum driving in a day for work: [TO CONFIRM: maximum daily driving hours]. Maximum combined driving and clinical work in a day: [TO CONFIRM: maximum combined working hours].

6.4 Do not schedule a full clinical load on top of a long drive, and do not drive home after a day that has already run long. Opal will pay for overnight accommodation rather than have you drive tired: [TO CONFIRM: the distance or time threshold at which overnight accommodation is approved, and who approves it].

6.5 If you are too tired to drive safely, stop. Phone your supervisor. This will always be supported.

7. TRANSPORTING PARTICIPANTS

[TO CONFIRM: whether Opal clinicians may transport participants in their own vehicle. If it is permitted, this section must set out the insurance position, when it is permitted, consent and documentation, restraint and wheelchair transport requirements, and who may be present.]

Where transporting participants is not permitted, that is because the insurance, restraint and safeguarding considerations are substantial. Community access transport belongs in a participant's plan with a provider set up for it.

8. PARKING AND ACCESS

Park where you can leave without reversing into traffic or being blocked in. Do not park in a driveway you would need someone else to move a car to exit. Parking costs incurred at a participant visit are reimbursable; a parking fine is not.

9. AFTER A CRASH OR AN INCIDENT

1. Stop. Check for injuries and call 000 if anyone is hurt.
2. Exchange details with the other driver. Do not admit liability.
3. Photograph the scene, the vehicles and the damage.
4. Call the police where required — anyone is injured, a vehicle is towed, or the other driver refuses details.
5. Tell your supervisor as soon as it is safe to.
6. Report it as an incident in the portal within 24 hours, and follow the Injury Management System information for workers if you were hurt.

Report near misses too. A near miss on a rural road at the end of a long day is telling you something about the schedule, not about the driver.

title: Injury Management System — information for workers
summary: The document section 159 of the Workers Compensation and Injury Management Act 2023 (WA) requires Opal Therapy to make available to workers — how to claim, what Opal does, who is responsible for injury management, and how a dispute is resolved.
body:
INJURY MANAGEMENT SYSTEM — INFORMATION FOR WORKERS

Why you are being given this. Section 159 of the Workers Compensation and Injury Management Act 2023 (WA) requires an employer to establish and maintain an injury management system, and to describe it in a document made available to workers. This is that document. The content it must cover is prescribed by regulation, including naming the person responsible for injury management and how to contact them.

1. WHAT AN INJURY MANAGEMENT SYSTEM IS FOR

Two things. Making sure you get the treatment and the income support you are entitled to, and helping you get back to safe work — which for most injuries is the thing that most improves recovery, not a reward for having recovered.

Workers compensation cover is Opal's obligation and Opal's cost. You are never asked to hold or pay for it.

2. WHO IS RESPONSIBLE

Person responsible for injury management at Opal: [TO CONFIRM: name, role, phone and email of the person responsible for injury management — required content under regulation 73]
Alternative contact: [TO CONFIRM: name and contact]
Opal's workers compensation insurer: [TO CONFIRM: insurer name, policy number and claims contact]

3. WHAT TO DO IF YOU ARE INJURED AT WORK

3.1 Get treatment. In an emergency call 000. Otherwise see a doctor as soon as you can. You may choose your own treating doctor.

3.2 Tell Opal as soon as possible — the same day where you can, and before the end of your shift. Report to your supervisor and to the person named in section 2. Report even if you think the injury is minor: an injury that seems small at the time and is never reported becomes very difficult to claim for later.

3.3 Report it as an incident in the portal within 24 hours, under the Incident Management Policy.

3.4 If you want to claim, ask your doctor for a WorkCover WA First Certificate of Capacity. Give it to Opal with a completed claim form.

3.5 Opal will forward your claim to the insurer within the statutory timeframe — [TO CONFIRM: verify the current forwarding timeframe under the Workers Compensation and Injury Management Act 2023 (WA) and state it here]. Opal will not delay a claim because it disagrees with it, and disputing liability is the insurer's decision to make, not ours.

3.6 The insurer decides liability within the period the Act allows and will write to you. If liability is disputed, you keep your rights under section 7.

4. WHAT OPAL WILL DO

• Give you this document, a claim form and any help you need to complete it.
• Forward your claim and certificates to the insurer within the statutory timeframe.
• Nominate and pay for injury management support where the injury requires it.
• Develop a return to work programme with you and your treating doctor where your certificate says you have some capacity for work.
• Offer suitable duties where they are reasonably practicable — modified tasks, reduced hours, a different location, or administrative work while you recover.
• Keep your medical information confidential and share it only with those who need it for the claim or your return to work.
• Keep in contact with you while you are off work, and keep it supportive rather than pressuring.
• Not dismiss you because of a work-related injury within the protected period the Act provides, and not treat you unfavourably for making a claim.

5. WHAT WE ASK OF YOU

• Report the injury promptly, and report it accurately.
• Provide certificates of capacity on time, and keep providing them while you are receiving payments.
• Attend medical appointments and follow reasonable treatment.
• Take part in developing your return to work programme, and try the suitable duties offered where your doctor has approved them.
• Tell us if your capacity changes, in either direction.
• Tell us if a return to work arrangement is not working. It can be changed.

6. RETURN TO WORK

A return to work programme is written where your treating doctor certifies partial capacity. It names the duties, the hours, the restrictions, who is supervising the arrangement, and the review dates. It is developed with you — not handed to you — and reviewed as your capacity changes.

Suitable duties are real work adjusted to your capacity, not a token task. Where Opal cannot reasonably provide suitable duties, we will say so and explain why.

7. IF YOU DISAGREE WITH SOMETHING

Raise it with the person named in section 2 first, if you feel able to.

You can also contact:
• WorkCover WA — advice on your rights, and the conciliation and arbitration services that resolve workers compensation disputes: 1300 794 744, workcover.wa.gov.au
• Your union or a lawyer, at any stage.

Using any of these will not affect how you are treated at Opal.

8. INJURIES THAT ARE NOT OBVIOUSLY INJURIES

This system covers psychological injury, gradual-onset musculoskeletal injury, and injury from a single exposure event as well as an obvious accident. A psychological injury arising from work is reportable and claimable on the same terms as a physical one, and Opal will treat it that way.

9. PRIVACY

Information about your injury and claim is used to manage the claim and your return to work. It is disclosed to the insurer, to the treating and assessing practitioners involved, and to those at Opal who need it. It is not shared with colleagues, and your diagnosis is not disclosed to your team.

title: Emergency and Disaster Management Policy
summary: What to do in a fire, a medical emergency, a bushfire or cyclone, an extreme heat day, a road closure or a system outage — and how Opal Therapy keeps supporting participants when normal service is not possible.
body:
EMERGENCY AND DISASTER MANAGEMENT POLICY

1. PURPOSE

Two obligations sit together here. Keeping workers safe in an emergency, and making sure participants who depend on a support do not simply lose it because conditions became difficult. The NDIS Practice Standards require providers to plan for both, and in Western Australia the realistic scenarios are bushfire, cyclone, flood, extreme heat, storm, a long road closure, an infectious disease event, and the loss of power, telecommunications or our own systems.

2. IN AN IMMEDIATE EMERGENCY

Call 000. Ask for fire, police or ambulance. State the address first — including the suburb and any landmark, because you may be cut off.

Your safety comes before everything else in this policy. You are not expected to put yourself at risk to continue a service.

3. MEDICAL EMERGENCY DURING A VISIT

1. Call 000.
2. Give first aid within your training. Do not attempt what you are not trained for.
3. Stay with the person until help arrives, unless staying is unsafe.
4. Get the participant's emergency information — the portal holds their emergency contacts, and their medication list if we have one — and give it to the paramedics.
5. Contact the emergency contact and your supervisor.
6. Write it up the same day and report it as an incident within 24 hours.

Take a mobile phone with charge to every visit. It is the first item on the list because everything above depends on it.

4. FIRE

In the office: raise the alarm, call 000, evacuate by the nearest safe exit, do not use lifts, go to the assembly point at [TO CONFIRM: office assembly point], and do not re-enter until told it is safe. Only attempt to fight a fire if it is small, you are trained, and you have a clear exit behind you.

In a participant's home: get everyone out first, including the participant — which may need planning if they have mobility or sensory needs. Call 000 from outside.

Office emergency arrangements — wardens, extinguishers, evacuation diagram, drill frequency: [TO CONFIRM: office emergency arrangements and who maintains them].

5. BUSHFIRE

5.1 Check the Emergency WA website and the Bureau of Meteorology before travelling to any regional or bushland area during the fire season, and check again before you leave a location.

5.2 Do not travel into an area under a Watch and Act or Emergency Warning. Do not attempt to drive through smoke. A road that was open this morning may not be open this afternoon.

5.3 On a Catastrophic fire danger rating day, visits in affected areas do not proceed. This is not a judgement call to be made at the roadside: [TO CONFIRM: who makes the call to cancel visits on a high fire danger day, and by when].

5.4 If you are caught: do not drive through fire, do not shelter in the open, and follow the advice broadcast for the area. Call 000 and tell your supervisor where you are.

6. CYCLONE, STORM AND FLOOD

Follow DFES advice for the region. Do not drive through floodwater under any circumstances, at any depth. Where a cyclone warning is issued for an area we service, visits are suspended and participants are contacted under section 9.

7. EXTREME HEAT

Heat is a genuine risk both to you and to participants, particularly those with limited mobility, some medications, or no air conditioning. On a day forecast above [TO CONFIRM: temperature threshold]: schedule visits early, carry water, do not sit in a parked car, and check on participants known to be at risk. Consider telehealth instead of a long drive.

8. LOSS OF SYSTEMS

If the portal, phones or internet are unavailable: continue seeing participants, keep contemporaneous notes on paper, and enter them into the portal as soon as it is back — recording the actual date of the contact and the date of entry, as the Clinical Documentation Policy requires. Do not use personal accounts or unapproved tools as a workaround.
Who to contact during an outage, and the backup contact method: [TO CONFIRM: outage contact and backup communication method].

9. CONTINUING TO SUPPORT PARTICIPANTS

9.1 Opal maintains a list of participants whose supports cannot safely be interrupted, and who is responsible for contacting each of them when normal service is disrupted: [TO CONFIRM: who maintains the priority participant list and who makes the calls].

9.2 During a disruption, participants are contacted, told what is happening, and offered an alternative where one is safe — telehealth, a phone review, a rescheduled visit, or a referral for something urgent.

9.3 Participants' own emergency plans are part of our clinical work with them. Where a participant relies on power for equipment, has limited mobility, or would not be able to evacuate without help, that belongs in their plan and should be discussed with them and their other providers before a season, not during one.

10. AFTER

Everyone involved is checked on, offered a debrief, and offered support through [TO CONFIRM: employee assistance programme details, or a note that none is currently provided]. The event is reviewed: what worked, what did not, and what changes before next time.

title: Conflict of Interest Policy
summary: How to recognise and declare a conflict between your own interests and a participant's, including the conflicts specific to NDIS practice — recommending equipment, referring to a related provider, and holding more than one role for the same person.
body:
CONFLICT OF INTEREST POLICY

1. PURPOSE

A participant relies on our recommendation being about them. A conflict of interest is anything that could reasonably be seen to compromise that — and the test is the appearance, not only the reality, because a participant cannot see inside your reasoning and should not have to.

Having a conflict is not misconduct. Failing to declare one is.

2. THE THREE KINDS

2.1 Actual — your interests and the participant's genuinely diverge right now.
2.2 Potential — they could diverge if circumstances change.
2.3 Perceived — a reasonable person, knowing the facts, could think your judgement was affected. This one is declared on exactly the same terms as the others.

3. THE CONFLICTS THAT ACTUALLY ARISE IN THIS PRACTICE

3.1 Equipment and assistive technology. Recommending a product where you, a family member or Opal receive a commission, discount, rebate, sponsorship, referral fee or other benefit from the supplier. Also: a supplier relationship that has become comfortable enough that you stop comparing options.

3.2 Referrals within a group. Referring to another service that Opal, an owner or a relative has an interest in, without telling the participant that connection exists and without offering alternatives.

3.3 Multiple roles for one participant. Acting as both their therapist and their support coordinator, plan manager or behaviour support practitioner. The NDIS Practice Standards treat this as a conflict to be managed transparently, and Opal treats it as one to be avoided where it reasonably can be.

3.4 Assessment and provision. Writing the functional capacity or equipment report that recommends a service Opal then delivers. This is common and often unavoidable in a small practice. It must be disclosed to the participant in writing, and the report must stand on evidence a different clinician would reach the same way.

3.5 Personal relationships. Providing services to a friend, a relative, a neighbour or a former partner. Employing, supervising or making decisions about a person you have a close personal relationship with. Being involved in a hiring decision about a friend or relative.

3.6 Outside work. Private practice, other employment, consultancy, teaching, a board position, or a business that competes with Opal or draws on Opal's participants, systems or information.

3.7 Gifts, hospitality and benefits. Including supplier-funded conferences, meals, product training and travel. See the Gifts and Benefits Policy.

3.8 Financial involvement with a participant. Prohibited outright — see the Professional Boundaries Policy.

4. YOUR OBLIGATIONS

4.1 Declare it as soon as you become aware of it. Not at the end of the episode of care, and not when someone asks.

4.2 Declare in writing to your supervisor and to [TO CONFIRM: the role or register where conflict declarations are recorded]. Say what the interest is, who it affects, and what you propose to do about it.

4.3 Declare on commencement, when anything changes, and at [TO CONFIRM: annual declaration cycle, if one is adopted].

4.4 Do not act on the matter until you have been told how it is being managed, unless waiting would harm the participant.

4.5 When you are uncertain whether something counts, declare it. The cost of an unnecessary declaration is five minutes.

5. HOW A CONFLICT IS MANAGED

In rough order of preference: avoid it — reallocate the participant or the decision; restrict it — remove yourself from the specific decision while continuing the rest of the work; disclose and monitor it — tell the participant plainly, in writing, offer them genuine alternatives, and have the decision reviewed independently.

Disclosure alone is the weakest control and is not enough on its own for a significant conflict.

Whatever is decided is recorded, along with who decided it.

6. WHAT THE PARTICIPANT MUST BE TOLD

Where a conflict affects a participant, they are told plainly: what the connection is, what alternatives exist, that they may choose a different provider or supplier, and that their supports will not be affected by that choice. In writing, in a form they can use, and recorded in their file.

7. PROCUREMENT AND SUPPLIER RELATIONSHIPS

Compare options for any significant equipment recommendation and record the comparison in the participant's file — what was considered, what was recommended, and why. Do not accept a benefit from a supplier that is conditional on volume or on recommending their product. Report any offer of a commission or referral fee.

8. BREACHES

An undeclared conflict that affects a participant's care or Opal's funding is a serious disciplinary matter and may be reportable to the NDIS Commission or AHPRA. As with everything else here, declaring late is far better than not declaring.

title: Home Visit & Community Work Safety Policy
summary: How to stay safe working in participants' homes, schools and community settings — the pre-visit screen, the arrival assessment, animals, other people present, and your unconditional right to leave.
body:
HOME VISIT & COMMUNITY WORK SAFETY POLICY

1. PURPOSE

A participant's home is their home. It is also, while you are working in it, a workplace Opal has a duty to make safe so far as is reasonably practicable — and one we cannot inspect, control or modify in advance. This policy is how that duty is met in a place that belongs to someone else.

2. THE OVERRIDING RULE

You may leave any visit, at any time, for any safety reason, without seeking approval and without explaining yourself first. Report it afterwards. You will never be criticised, and you will never be asked to go back before the concern is addressed.

Nothing about a participant's needs, a report deadline, a funding period or an inconvenienced family outweighs this.

3. BEFORE THE FIRST VISIT

3.1 Environmental risk screen. Complete one for every new participant before the first home visit, and record it in the portal. It covers: known aggression or behaviours of concern, whoever else lives in or visits the home, animals, drug or alcohol use, weapons, smoking indoors, hoarding, structural or electrical hazards, access and parking, mobile coverage, and any history of an incident at the address.

3.2 Where the screen identifies significant risk, the first visit is a joint visit, or is held in a neutral setting, or does not proceed until a control is in place. Your supervisor decides that with you, not for you.

3.3 Re-screen when something changes — a new household member, a change in behaviour, a relationship breakdown, a bereavement, a relapse.

4. BEFORE YOU LEAVE THE OFFICE OR HOME

• Check the participant's file, including alerts and the risk screen. Read them; do not assume you remember.
• Confirm the appointment and ask who will be home.
• Make sure your calendar shows the address and the expected finish time. Colleagues rely on it.
• Charge your phone. Take a charger.
• Follow the check-in arrangements in the Lone Worker Policy.
• Tell someone if you are going somewhere with poor coverage.

5. ARRIVING

5.1 Assess from the car before you get out. Look at who is around, whether there is shouting, whether there is a dog, whether you can get out again — do not park where you can be blocked in. Reverse into a driveway if you can, or park on the street facing your exit.

5.2 Take only what you need. Leave valuables locked out of sight, and lock the car.

5.3 At the door, note who answers and whether it matches what you expected. If someone unexpected is present, decide whether the visit still goes ahead. You may say you will come back another time.

5.4 If it feels wrong, it is wrong enough. Instinct in this setting is pattern recognition, not superstition. Leave and phone your supervisor from somewhere safe.

6. INSIDE

6.1 Know your exit. Sit or stand where you can reach a door without passing the other person. Do not let yourself be positioned in a back bedroom or a bathroom with no way past someone.

6.2 Keep your phone and keys on you, not in a bag across the room.

6.3 Watch for hazards as you work: trip hazards, wet floors, loose rugs, poor lighting, unstable furniture, exposed wiring, heaters, and anything you are being asked to lift.

6.4 Animals. Ask for dogs to be secured before you arrive and again on arrival. Do not enter a yard with a loose dog. Do not accept "he's friendly" as a control. Record any animal risk in the file.

6.5 Smoking. Ask for smoking to stop during the visit; that is a reasonable request and it is about your health as well as the participant's. If it continues, shorten the visit, move outside, or reschedule.

6.6 Other people. Family members, support workers, visitors. Be clear about who is present, and if someone is intoxicated, aggressive or intimidating, end the visit.

6.7 Weapons. Firearms, knives kept for protection, or anything used to threaten. Leave immediately and report. Never attempt to remove or secure a weapon.

6.8 Manual handling. Do not lift or transfer a person alone where the plan requires two people or equipment. Do not improvise a transfer because equipment has not arrived.

7. WHEN SOMETHING HAPPENS

7.1 Immediate danger — leave. Call 000 from a safe place. Do not stay to de-escalate, and do not go back for your equipment.

7.2 Aggression short of danger — end the visit calmly. Do not argue, do not raise your voice, do not turn your back, and do not warn the person about consequences. Leave, then phone your supervisor.

7.3 Report everything, including the ones where nothing actually happened. Near misses are what let us fix an address before someone is hurt at it.

8. AFTER A DIFFICULT VISIT

Tell your supervisor the same day. You will be offered a debrief, and support through [TO CONFIRM: employee assistance programme details, or a note that none is currently provided]. Opal will review whether and how the service continues, including a joint-visit requirement, a change of setting, or ending the service. That decision is not yours to carry alone.

9. SCHOOLS AND COMMUNITY SETTINGS

Follow the site's own sign-in, visitor and emergency procedures, and ask on arrival where the exits and assembly point are. Confirm what checks the site requires of you before you attend — see the onboarding checklist for the checks that apply to your role. Everything in this policy about assessing the environment and leaving if it is unsafe applies equally.
